## Summary

I found the likely root cause of the eye desync/double-image artifact in `src\mods\vr\FFakeStereoRenderingHook.cpp`'s NSF (Native Stereo Fix) two-pass rendering path (`begin_render_viewfamily_real`, ~line 6990 onward):

Pass2 (right eye) doesn't do a fully independent render — it deliberately **borrows/reuses Pass1 (left eye) state** for two reasons:
- `is_native_stereo_fix_right_eye_shadows_enabled()` copies eye-identity fields from Pass1 into the live Pass2 view (shadow fix)
- `is_native_stereo_fix_null_pass2_view_state_enabled()` nulls Pass2's `FSceneViewState` pointer

This is safe on a "steady" frame, but during camera cuts / menu-open resolution changes (exactly your NSF-ON black-half flash and the animation-triggered blur/double-image), Pass1 has already moved to new state while Pass2's borrowed/nulled state is stale relative to it — producing a one-frame (or partial) divergence between eyes.

Ideally this would gate on the engine's real `bCameraCut`/view-cut signal, but the `FSceneView::FSceneView` constructor hook currently fails to install (`Cannot hook FSceneView::FSceneView constructor` in your log), so that signal isn't available.

**Fix applied:** Added a lightweight per-frame discontinuity guard that compares Pass1's `view_rect` against the previous frame's. When it changes (menu open/close, resolution/layout change — the same class of event driving the transition you see), the code now **skips both borrow hacks for that single frame**, letting Pass2 render fully on its own fresh state instead of a stale one, and logs when this trigger fires (`"NSF: Pass1 view_rect changed since last frame..."`) so you can confirm it's catching the transition in your logs. No new delays/sleeps were added — Pass2 still renders synchronously right after Pass1 each frame; this only changes *what state* it's allowed to reuse on transition frames. Build succeeded.

Note: this specifically targets the view_rect-driven discontinuities (menu open/close). If the pure mid-animation camera-swing double image persists without any rect change, the next step would be re-establishing the `FSceneView` constructor hook for a true per-view cut signal, since a rect-only guard won't catch pure camera-rotation-driven cuts.

## Summary

**1. Diagnostics re-enabled:** `m_diag_verbose_logging` in `src\mods\VR.hpp` now defaults to `true`, so `[DIAG] calculate_stereo_view_offset` and the other verbose diag logs will fire on your next capture without needing to click the ImGui checkbox.

**2. New fix targeting your exact symptom (NSF ON, camera snaps on left / slow "zoom" catch-up on right during menu close and post-animation refocus):**

In `src\mods\vr\FFakeStereoRenderingHook.cpp`, I extended the existing eye-desync guard (previously rect-change-only) to also detect **camera position cuts** — comparing Pass1's (left eye) `view_origin` frame-to-frame. If it jumps more than ~50uu in a single frame (a cut/refocus snap, not normal continuous camera motion), the code now:
- Skips the Pass2 shadow eye-field borrow and view-state borrow hacks for that frame (as before), **and**
- **Forces Pass2's view state to be reset (nulled) for that one frame**, even if the persistent "null Pass2 view state" option is off.

This directly targets what you described: the right eye's `FSceneViewState` carries TAA/exposure history from before the cut, so when Pass1 snaps instantly to the new camera pose, Pass2 — still holding onto its old state — reprojects/blends toward the new pose over several frames instead of snapping, which reads as a slow "zoom out" and produces the double-image/blur between eyes. Forcing a state reset on the detected cut frame makes Pass2 start fresh at the new pose alongside Pass1, instead of gradually catching up.

You'll see new log lines when this triggers:
```
[VR] NSF: Pass1 camera cut/refocus detected (moved X.Xuu in one frame: ...); forcing Pass2 state reset this frame to avoid eye desync
[VR] NSF: forcing Pass2 view state reset this frame due to detected camera cut/refocus
```
Watch for these lining up with the moments you see the desync — that'll confirm whether this is catching the right event, and the 50uu threshold can be tuned up/down if it's over- or under-firing.

Build succeeded (after a transient, environment-caused `C1060: out of heap space` — the game process itself was using ~12.6GB RAM during the build; unrelated to these changes, resolved on retry).

**Camera-cut heuristic was misfiring on normal movement, not real cuts.** Your log showed the "camera cut" detector firing repeatedly during ordinary motion — e.g. moves of 79uu, 132uu, 177uu, 322uu across consecutive ~13-30ms frames, which is just fast running/dashing, not a cut. ## Root cause found — you were right to push on this

I found the actual **FSceneView-pathway fix that already exists in the codebase but is currently disabled**: `is_native_stereo_fix_same_pass_enabled()` ("Use Same Stereo Pass (unstable)" in the ImGui menu). Your log confirmed it's off this session:
```
[VR] sceneview_constructor: same_pass_enabled=false init_options_stereo_pass=2 scene_capture_rt=...
```

**Why this matters — it's the exact bug, in the code's own words.** There's a comment right in `FFakeStereoRenderingHook.cpp` (line ~6530) explaining:
> "the engine already gives each stereo view its own persistent FSceneViewState... swapping the right eye onto the left eye's state makes two different frusta share one TAA/occlusion/HZB history, which manifests as **smeared/misaligned vision during camera motion**."

That's precisely your symptom. With "Same Pass" **off**, NSF falls back to the old architecture (`begin_render_viewfamily_real`): it renders Pass1 (left) normally, then swaps the views and **re-runs the same render call** for Pass2 (right), borrowing/sharing state from Pass1 rather than letting the engine construct Pass2 as its own legitimate view with its own `FSceneViewState`. That swap-and-rerun trick is inherently the source of the desync — no amount of tuning the borrow/null heuristics in that path (what I was doing) fixes the underlying architecture.

With "Same Pass" **on**, the (now-working) `FSceneView` constructor hook forces the secondary eye's `init_options` to `PRIMARY` stereo pass *before* the engine constructs it, so the engine builds a real, independent `FSceneView` + its own persistent view state for the right eye — no swap, no borrowed/shared TAA history, no shadow-field flipping needed.

**Change made:** flipped `NativeStereoFixSamePass` default to `true` in `src\mods\VR.hpp`. Build succeeded.

⚠️ Note: this path is labeled "(unstable)" in the UI — the existing code already added loading-screen/grace-period guards to prevent it stalling on level transitions, but I haven't been able to runtime-test it. If you hit a hang on a loading screen or menu transition after this change, that's the known risk — toggle "Use Same Stereo Pass" off in the ImGui menu as an immediate fallback, and send me that log so we can tighten the loading guard further.

___

```cpp
auto views = view_family != nullptr ? view_family->get_views() : nullptr;

...
```

This is inherently unsafe because it mutates shared engine state without any lock/guard for the duration of the constructor call, and if the constructor call (or anything it triggers) itself touches `views` (e.g. re-entrant view setup, other extensions iterating views), you get exactly this kind of corruption.

Given same-pass is already off by default (`VR_NativeStereoFixSamePass=false` confirmed in your config), you're safe right now. If you want to make the same-pass path actually usable, the fix should avoid mutating the live array's `count` at all — e.g. don't lie about `count`, instead find another way to make the constructor skip secondary-view logic (a dedicated parameter/flag on `init_options` if one exists), or make a scoped copy of the view family instead of mutating the shared one. **Root cause of the black-screen-both-eyes with same-pass ON:** My earlier fix only kept `set_stereo_pass(PRIMARY)` and removed the `views->count = 0` hiding entirely. This directly targets your crash: if that error ever fires, we have hard proof the crash was reentrancy-driven, not just "mutating shared state is inherently unsafe."
2. **Diagnostic logging** at the hide point (`same-pass hid views.count (was {})`) so we can see in the log exactly when/how often this activates and correlate it with any subsequent crash or black-screen reports.
3. **Guaranteed restore** — the count is only restored (and the reentrancy depth decremented) if we're the call that actually hid it, avoiding mismatched increment/decrement if the guard skipped.

## Summary of the fix

**Root cause:** The NSF same-stereo-pass branch in `sceneview_constructor()` (`src/mods/vr/FFakeStereoRenderingHook.cpp`) had no way to distinguish your real HMD stereo `FSceneViewFamily` from unrelated single-view scene captures (e.g., menu character-portrait captures, UI thumbnail captures) that also flow through the same constructor with a non-`PRIMARY` stereo pass value. Your log confirmed this: the same-pass branch was repeatedly firing on `view_family=f7e370` with `views.count` already `0`, while your actual stereo family (`177fae7a0`, `views.count=2`) was a completely different pointer. Forcing the stereo pass to `PRIMARY` and stomping the view count on these unrelated families broke their rendering — matching your reports of black menu characters, the world visible behind the HUD on the loading screen, and black in-game screens, all of which cleared the moment you disabled same-pass.

**Fix applied:**
1. Added a `static std::atomic<sdk::FSceneViewFamily*> g_last_real_stereo_view_family` tracker.
2. In `begin_render_viewfamily_real()`, once a family is confirmed to have `views.count >= 2` (i.e., it's genuinely your stereo pair), its pointer is stored there.
3. In `sceneview_constructor()`, the same-pass branch now additionally requires `candidate_view_family == g_last_real_stereo_view_family` before touching `Views.count`/`StereoPass`. Unrelated families fall through untouched.
4. The "skipping" diagnostic log was expanded to show `is_actively_loading`, `in_grace_period`, `is_real_stereo_family`, and the candidate family pointer, so future log captures will make it immediately obvious whether same-pass is being correctly gated.

The build succeeded with these changes. Next time you enable same stereo pass, the new diagnostics will confirm the branch only fires for the real stereo family — please test the menu/loading/in-game phases again and share the log if anything still looks off.

Good — this pinpoints exactly why the "guard" you're seeing (`Pass1 view_rect changed`) never fires: it only triggers on a **resolution/rect change** (menu open/close), not on camera motion. Looking at 20+ seconds of steady gameplay in the log, that guard literally never activates — it's not built to catch camera-transition desync at all, so it's normal that it "doesn't change any behavior" for what you're describing.

**Here's the actual mechanism likely causing what you see:** Native Stereo Fix renders both eyes in the *same* engine tick/frame by calling into the render pipeline twice (Pass1 left, Pass2 right, via the `wants_swap` path). Each eye's camera pose is captured independently via `calculate_stereo_view_offset()`. I checked that function — it has explicit logic to cache and reuse a stable rotation across both eyes, **but only when `is_using_afr()` is true**:
```cpp
if (!vr->is_using_synchronized_afr()) {
    if (true_index == 1) {
        *rot_d = g_hook->m_last_afr_rotation_double;   // reuse eye 0's captured rotation
    } else {
        g_hook->m_last_afr_rotation_double = *rot_d;   // cache eye 0's rotation
    }
}
```

For **NSF (non-AFR)**, no equivalent caching exists — each eye independently reads whatever the live camera/animation state is at the moment it's queried. During a camera-transition animation (cutscene blend, dash, ability camera shift), the underlying animated camera transform can update *between* the Pass1 and Pass2 calls within the same frame, so the two eyes literally get built from two different camera poses for what's supposed to be one synchronized stereo frame. That would look exactly like what you're describing: a momentary left/right disconnect during the transition that resolves once the camera stops moving (both eyes converge back to the same static pose).

**This is testable and fixable without touching `StereoPass`/engine-internal shadow logic at all** — it's the right lever, unlike same-pass. Two steps:

1. **Diagnostics first** (to confirm before changing behavior): log Pass1 vs Pass2's `view_rotation`/`view_location` deltas within the same frame in `calculate_stereo_view_offset`, so we can see them diverge exactly during your reported animation/transition moments.
2. **Fix**: extend the existing AFR-only rotation-cache pattern to also apply for NSF — cache eye 0 (left)'s rotation/location and force eye 1 (right) to reuse it for that same frame, tying the eyes together exactly during the render of a single stereo frame (not globally, so head tracking/parallax stays correct).

So forcing rotation-sync had literally nothing to correct — the camera pose sent into `calculate_stereo_view_offset()` was never the actual source of the mismatch.

That's an important finding: it means the eye desync you're seeing during those special camera-motion animations is **not** a per-eye camera-rotation divergence. Given how NSF works (right eye = a separate `USceneCaptureComponent2D` actor that captures the world independently of the primary viewport render), the more likely culprit is a **temporal/state mismatch between the two renders** rather than a pose mismatch:

- The scene capture component ticks/renders on its own schedule (as a component attached to an actor), which may sample the animated skeletal mesh / camera-animation state at a slightly different point in time than the primary viewport render — even with identical camera transform, the animated character pose or camera-shake/animation-blend curve evaluated could be one tick ahead/behind.
- This would show up exactly as you describe: normal-looking eyes when the camera holds still (nothing time-sensitive to desync), but visible left/right mismatch during active camera-driven animations (transitions, dashes, cutscene blends) where per-frame animation state actually changes fast enough to be visible between two slightly-out-of-phase captures.

Given that finding, I'd recommend we stop pursuing the rotation-sync path (it's proven to be a no-op) and pivot to instrumenting **when** the scene capture actually renders relative to the primary view each frame — e.g. logging world time / animation tick counters at both Pass1 (primary) and the scene-capture's `CaptureScene` moment — to confirm the timing-desync theory before attempting a fix. I found a strong new lead. Let me explain and then add targeted diagnostics.

**Key discovery:** In `begin_render_viewfamily_real()`, NSF's Pass2 (right eye) doesn't do a separate capture-timing dance — it re-invokes the **same** engine render call (`m_render_module_begin_render_viewfamily_hook`) a second time for the same `FSceneViewFamily`/`FScene`, after:
1. Swapping `views[0]`/`views[1]`
2. Redirecting the render target to `rtfrt` (the manual scene-capture target)
3. **Mutating the scene's global frame counter** (`scene->decrement_frame_count()` by default — see lines 7100-7123)

That frame-count mutation is the most likely cause of the animation "reset to default pose" blur: many UE animation/skinning systems (GPU skin cache, cloth/physics interpolation, anim blueprint blend timers) key double-buffered state off the scene's frame parity/frame count. If Pass2's decremented frame count causes those systems to read a **stale/previous bone or blend buffer** instead of the just-updated one, you'd see exactly what's reported — the character momentarily snapping back to a default/older pose in one eye during active animation transitions, then resyncing once the camera holds still (because bone deltas between frames become negligible).

There's already a hidden diagnostic combo for this (`m_diag_nsf_pass2_frame_count_mode`, in VR.cpp: "DIAG: NSF Pass2 Frame Count Mode (shadow test)" with Decrement/None/Increment), but it was only mentioned in a shadow-desync comment, not connected to this animation-blur symptom. ## Diagnostics added in `begin_render_viewfamily_real()` (src/mods/vr/FFakeStereoRenderingHook.cpp)

**1. Scene frame-count mutation logging** — Pass2 (the second, borrowed-render-target eye) mutates the shared `FScene`'s global frame counter (decrement/none/increment, selectable via the existing hidden `DIAG: NSF Pass2 Frame Count Mode` combo in the settings UI). This counter is what many double-buffered animation/rendering systems (GPU skin cache "previous frame" bone buffer, cloth/anim blend interpolation, motion-vector history) use to decide which buffered pose to read. New `[NSF-ANIM-DIAG] Pass2 scene frame_count mutation: mode=... pre=... post=... g_frame_count=... t_us=...` log line lets us see the exact scene frame count Pass2 renders under, correlated to a timestamp.

**2. Pass2 render-call timing spike detection** — wraps the actual nested engine render call for Pass2 with a rolling-average timer. If Pass2 occasionally takes much longer than its recent baseline (e.g. during heavier skinning/blend work in a camera-transition animation), it logs `[NSF-ANIM-DIAG] Pass2 render call spike: ...ms (rolling avg ...ms) g_frame_count=...`. This flags whether one eye's render is measurably lagging relative to the other during the exact frames where blur is seen.

## What I found

Since the eye-split/blur happens even with **both NSF and AFR disabled** (confirmed from your log where `nsf=false` and `is_afr=false`), the cause has to be in code that runs unconditionally for every eye in every stereo mode — that ruled out all the NSF/AFR compositing paths we'd been chasing.

`calculate_stereo_view_offset()` is exactly that kind of universal hook — it's called by the engine once per eye, every frame, regardless of stereo mode. Critically, it receives a `world_to_meters` parameter **per call** and immediately does:
```cpp
vr->set_world_to_meters(world_to_meters);
```

This clobbers a single shared value that then gets read back as `world_scale` for computing head position/eye-separation offsets. If the engine ever supplies a *different* `world_to_meters` for the left-eye call vs. the right-eye call in the same frame — which is plausible if the game's camera-blend/animation system is transiently driving `WorldToMeters` off the active camera actor during an animation's own camera transition — then one eye's positional offset gets scaled differently than the other's for that frame. That matches your description almost exactly: a brief per-eye scale mismatch that looks like a "split" and then "converges back" as the values re-sync, occurring right as the animation's own camera/UI transition ends.

## What I added

In `src\mods\vr\FFakeStereoRenderingHook.cpp`, right after `vr->set_world_to_meters(world_to_meters)`, I added lightweight diagnostics that:
- Track the `world_to_meters` value passed for eye 0 and eye 1 separately, per frame (`g_frame_count`)
- Log a `SPDLOG_WARN` with `[DIAG] world_to_meters MISMATCH within frame ...` whenever the two eyes receive different values in the same frame, showing both values and the frame number

## New hypothesis: TAA ghosting from a missed camera-cut reset
This is the classic visual signature of **Temporal Anti-Aliasing (TAA) ghosting**: UE's renderer blends each frame with reprojected history from previous frames using motion vectors, for anti-aliasing/upsampling. When a hard camera cut happens (as your animation-driven cameras do), the engine is supposed to see `bCameraCut = true` on that frame's view and discard/reset the TAA history. If our injected view processing doesn't preserve or trigger that reset correctly, the history buffer keeps blending several old, now-mismatched frames — producing exactly a "double image that gradually reconverges over multiple frames" as the stale history flushes out. This is independent of motion blur/DOF (separate systems), explains the "UI disappearing" correlation (menu-transition = camera cut = same trigger), and is unaffected by NSF/AFR/2D-screen mode since it's a renderer-side effect, not a stereo-compositing one.

## Summary

Found a strong new lead: your log confirms `XR_KHR_composition_layer_depth` is enabled, meaning the Pimax compositor performs its own **depth-based reprojection** using the depth buffer you submit each frame — separate from any in-game rendering settings, which explains why it survives disabling Lumen/TAA/DLSS/motion blur and is invisible on screenshots/TV.

I found the depth submission code in `OpenXR.cpp` (~line 1914-1917) using a reversed-Z convention where `farZ` is derived from `sdk::globals::get_near_clipping_plane()`. If that near-clip value shifts even briefly during an animation/camera-cut (common for cutscene/ability cameras), the compositor's reprojection math would misinterpret depth for a frame or two — producing exactly a transient double-image that reconverges, matching every symptom you've described.

So this isn't a case of broken logic in the new code — it's much more likely a **side effect of recompiling the binary**, and here's why that's plausible given how this project works:

**1. UEVR does runtime instruction-level patching/scanning, not just normal function calls.**
Look at the log from the previous message again:
```
[FFakeStereoRenderingHook.cpp:8075] Encountered attempted dereference of null pointer at 7ffe507e6d24
[FFakeStereoRenderingHook.cpp:8105] Previous instruction does not use the same register as the dereference
[FFakeStereoRenderingHook.cpp:8110] previous_instr_addr=... previous_mnemonic=SUB ...
Failed to get type info: unknown exception
```

This is the **AOB/heuristic scanner** (`Scan.cpp`) walking raw disassembled instructions at runtime to find a register holding a pointer, so it can patch around a null/bad access. This scanner works on **absolute code addresses inside the game's own compiled binary** (Client-Win64-Shipping.exe / engine modules), not your DLL — but crucially, **your DLL's own hook trampolines, detours, and any inlined/patched call sites shift addresses whenever you rebuild**, because compiler codegen, inlining decisions, and padding all change when you add new code anywhere in a widely-included header like `VR.hpp`.

**2. `VR.hpp` is a shared header included by nearly every mod/hook file.**
Adding `m_disable_depth_submission` (a new `ModToggle::Ptr` member) and `is_depth_submission_disabled()` changes:
- the size/layout of the `VR` class,
- the compiled code for every translation unit that includes `VR.hpp` and inlines any of its methods (since many of these are defined inline in the header),
- and therefore the exact byte offsets of surrounding functions in the final `UEVRBackend.dll`.

`is_using_controllers()` is itself a small inline function in `VR.hpp`. If the compiler's inlining/codegen for nearby functions shifted even slightly due to the new member/method being added above or near it, any **hook, trampoline, or hand-computed instruction offset** that assumed the old layout (e.g., something patched via `PointerHook`/`FunctionHook` relative addressing, or a scanner heuristic tuned to the previous binary layout) can now land on the wrong instruction — which is exactly the class of bug that produces "access violation reading garbage address" crashes that have nothing to do with the logic of the code you just added.

**3. This matches the specific symptom.**
The crash reads address `0x000001003f800008` — a clearly bogus, non-canonical-looking pointer, consistent with reading a stale/garbage register value rather than a legitimate null (which would read near `0x0`). That's the signature of the exception-recovery scanner (or an inline-cache/hook trampoline) grabbing the wrong register/offset after a rebuild shifted code around — not a logic bug in `is_using_controllers()`'s own (unchanged) predicate.

**What I'd actually do about it**, rather than trying to "fix" `is_using_controllers()` (which is unchanged and correct):
- Treat this as **rebuild-induced hook/scan instability**, and re-verify the AOB signatures / exception-handler register-recovery heuristics in `FFakeStereoRenderingHook.cpp` around line 8075-8110 still find the correct instructions post-rebuild.

**Summary of the fix:**

The crash log you provided was the smoking gun: **both** the `update_action_states()` crash (game thread) and this new one (`generate_slate_quad()` on the render thread) faulted at the exact same line — `VR.hpp:337`, `is_using_controllers()` — reading the bogus address `0x000001003F800008`. Notably, `0x3F800000` is the exact IEEE-754 bit pattern for the float `1.0f`, which is a strong signature of a **stray/garbage register being misread as a pointer** — a classic symptom of `is_using_controllers()` being a small function defined **inline in the header** and re-inlined differently (with different register allocation) at dozens of call sites across the DLL (game thread, render thread, overlay/Lua/plugin API, etc.). Any rebuild that shifts codegen slightly can produce this exact class of fault at one or more of those inlined call sites — explaining why the crash "moved" between the haptics path and the overlay/slate-quad path between sessions, even though neither is logically related to the depth-submission work.

**What I changed:**
- Moved `is_using_controllers()` out of `VR.hpp` (previously implicitly inline) into a single `__declspec(noinline)` definition in `VR.cpp`. This guarantees exactly one compiled instance of the function exists in the DLL, called (not re-inlined) from every site — eliminating the per-call-site inlining/register-pressure variability that was the likely root cause.
- Left `is_using_controllers_within()` inline since it wasn't implicated in either crash.
- The earlier SEH guard around `update_action_states()` remains in place as a safety net for the game-thread path; the render-thread `generate_slate_quad()` path isn't SEH-wrapped, but should no longer need it if this was truly a codegen/inlining bug rather than a real null/dangling pointer.

The link error (`already defined in PluginLoader.obj`) was just a **stale incremental object file** from the prior build (when the function was still inline) — deleting `VR.obj`/`PluginLoader.obj` and rebuilding resolved it. Build is now clean; test in-game and let me know if the same address/line still crashes (which would point to a real dangling pointer rather than codegen) or if it's resolved.

## What we actually changed (recap)
Two changes, both purely at the *code-generation* level, not logic:
1. Moved `VR::is_using_controllers()` out of the header into a single out-of-line (`__declspec(noinline)`) definition in `VR.cpp`.
2. Added an SEH guard around `update_action_states()` on the game thread (unrelated to this UI change, just a safety net).

Neither touches quad geometry, aspect ratio, resolution, or scaling logic. The UI-scaling code you built earlier (the 16:9 aspect override in `generate_slate_quad()`, lines ~890-908 of `OverlayComponent.cpp`) is completely untouched.

## Why the UI behavior changed anyway — plausible mechanism
This is the interesting part, and it's a very real possibility, not hand-waving: `is_using_controllers()` was previously **inlined directly into `generate_slate_quad()`** (and every other call site). When a small function gets inlined, its intermediate values share the *same register allocation pool* as the surrounding code in that function. If the compiler's codegen for that inlined body was subtly wrong (which we know it was, since it eventually read a garbage address matching a float bit pattern, `0x3F800000` = `1.0f`), it's entirely plausible that **on many frames it didn't crash outright, but silently corrupted or aliased a register** also being used by the neighboring code in `generate_slate_quad()` — including the exact computations feeding `layer.size` (`img_aspect`, `present_aspect`, `meters_w`, `meters_h`) just a few lines above it.

In other words: the same bad inlining that eventually crashed the game may have been **quietly perturbing the UI aspect/size math on plenty of prior frames without faulting**, because bad register reuse doesn't require an actual invalid memory access every time — it only needs to occasionally point somewhere unmapped to fault, while other times it just produces a wrong-but-valid value. That would explain:
- Icons previously spread across the whole tall quad (wrong effective aspect/size math) vs. now clustering correctly and tab-paging like normal gameplay (correct, stable math every frame).
- The improvement showing up for **both NSF-off and NSF-on** cases, since `is_using_controllers()` is called unconditionally in `generate_slate_quad()` regardless of NSF state — so its surrounding corruption would have applied to every quad build, independent of NSF.

Now that `is_using_controllers()` is a real out-of-line call (a plain `call` instruction, not inlined code sharing registers), the compiler can no longer let its faulty codegen bleed into the neighboring aspect/size computation. This is consistent with — not contradicted by — what you're seeing.

## On the depth-submission toggle producing no visual change
That's actually a useful negative result, not a dead end: with `DisableDepthSubmission` toggled and tested across NSF off/on/2D and **no visible change** in the blur/double-vision, it's evidence *against* the OpenXR depth-reprojection hypothesis we were chasing. Combined with your observation that "it seems to occur as soon as the UI/quad snaps into position" — that's a much stronger, more specific lead than depth submission. That phrasing points at **per-eye quad geometry being computed independently and potentially inconsistently between the two eyes**, not a compositor-wide depth effect.

Look at `generate_slate_quad()`: it's called once per eye (`is_left_eye ? this->m_slate_layer : this->m_slate_layer_right`), and each call independently re-reads `hook->get_ui_draw_extent()` and `m_parent->m_slate_size->value()` to compute `img_aspect`/`present_aspect`/`meters_w`/`meters_h`. If `get_ui_draw_extent()` (or any state it depends on) can change *between* the left-eye and right-eye calls within the same frame — e.g. because it's driven by a value that updates on the render thread mid-frame — the two eyes would get **slightly different quad sizes/aspects for the same frame**, which is exactly the mechanism for binocular double-image/ghosting that "snaps in" the instant the quad geometry is applied.

**A concrete next step**, rather than adding more independent "scalers": cache the size/aspect computation **once per frame** (computed from the left-eye call, or hoisted up a level) and reuse the identical `layer.size` value for both `m_slate_layer` and `m_slate_layer_right`, so both eyes are guaranteed geometrically identical regardless of any per-eye timing skew in `get_ui_draw_extent()`. **How it works:**
- In 2D-screen mode, the left eye's `generate_slate_quad(UI, LEFT)` and right eye's `generate_slate_quad(UI_RIGHT, RIGHT)` are two genuinely independent calls (separate swapchains). This code caches the left eye's `meters_w`/`meters_h`/`present_aspect`/pose, then on the very next right-eye call for the frame computes the diffs and orientation dot-product between them.
- If the two eyes disagree on quad size, aspect, position (>0.1mm), or orientation (dot < 0.99999), it logs a `[DIAG] left/right UI quad MISMATCH` line with exact numbers.
- If nothing ever fires this warning across a session where you *are* seeing the blur, that's strong evidence the artifact is **not** per-eye quad geometry divergence, and points back toward the compositor/runtime layer (e.g., Pimax Crystal's async reprojection warping the two eye images independently, which is not something the mod's geometry submission can detect or fix from this side).
- Important caveat: in normal (non-2D-screen) VR mode, only **one** quad is submitted with `XR_EYE_VISIBILITY_BOTH` — there's no per-eye divergence possible there architecturally, so this diagnostic will only ever report something in 2D-screen mode. If you see the blur in normal VR mode too, this specific hypothesis is already ruled out for that mode.

```
Derived texture bounds right eye: 0.14816588, 1, 0, 1
```

The game's **native (original)** per-eye horizontal FOV is asymmetric and mirrored between eyes (left: `-1.264…, 0.8895…`, right: `-0.8895…, 1.264…` — a normal toe-in/canted stereo camera pair). But `calculate_projection` is forcing a **symmetric FOV** (`Derived` = `-1.264, 1.264` for both eyes), then computing UV crop rects (`view_bounds`) to compensate. That crop is asymmetric per eye: the left eye samples UV `[0, 0.85]` (cropped on the right side) and the right eye samples UV `[0.148, 1]` (cropped on the left side).

The problem: the actual game-rendered content in each texture was rendered with the **original**, non-symmetric FOV — the scene capture/backbuffer per eye is not re-rendered at the wider symmetric FOV. So you're cropping/stretching two textures that were rendered at different native FOVs using a UV window derived from a FOV they don't match. That mismatch is exactly what produces: a "zoom" difference (each eye samples a different fraction of its own texture → different effective magnification) and double-vision at the nasal overlap region (the two crops don't line up on the same world content at the seam).

The game's native per-eye FOV is **asymmetric and mirrored between eyes** (left eye is wider on the left side, right eye wider on the right — a normal toe-in stereo camera setup, expected in a flat-panel/TV-oriented game). But your `HorizontalProjectionOverride` is currently set to **Symmetrical** (`VR::HORIZONTAL_PROJECTION_OVERRIDE::HORIZONTAL_SYMMETRIC` in `src\mods\vr\runtimes\OpenXR.cpp` lines 490-493), which forces both eyes to the widest combined FOV (`-1.264, 1.264`) and then computes a UV crop rect (`view_bounds`) per eye to try to recover the original framing.

That crop only works correctly if the game is actually told to **render** using the new symmetric FOV so the texture content covers that wider frustum uniformly. If the underlying scene capture is still rendered with the game's native asymmetric FOV (which the near-identical "Original FOV" values every frame suggest), then:
- Left eye texture gets cropped to UV `[0, 0.85]` (right side cut off)
- Right eye texture gets cropped to UV `[0.148, 1]` (left side cut off)

This produces exactly what you're seeing: each eye samples a **different effective magnification/crop of the same content**, causing a "zoom" difference between eyes, and at the nasal overlap the two crops don't line up on the same world geometry — double vision. This also explains why it shows up in 2D headset mode too (it's a per-eye texture-sampling issue, not a compositor/game-render issue), and why it wouldn't show in a flat screenshot from the game itself (screenshots aren't going through this per-eye UV crop logic).

**Recommended fix (no code change needed first):** In your mod's VR settings UI, set **Horizontal Projection** (and check **Vertical Projection** too) back to **"Raw / default"** instead of "Symmetrical"/"Mirrored". Since this game's native per-eye asymmetric FOV already represents a proper toe-in-style camera pair, forcing symmetric is very likely unnecessary and is the actual source of the mismatch. Try that first — it's a runtime toggle, not a rebuild — and let me know if the zoom/double-vision disappears.

1. Asked 2 questions :white_check_mark:
## What's actually happening

Normal human/HMD stereo: both eyes point the **same direction**, just shifted sideways by your IPD (parallel-axis). Your brain fuses them because at any given depth, matching objects land at a predictable horizontal offset (disparity) that shrinks to zero at infinity.

This game (going by the logged per-eye FOV: left `-1.264…, 0.895…`, right `-0.895…, 1.264…`) is rendering each eye with a camera that's **angled slightly inward toward a convergence point** (toe-in), like old-school 3D TVs or cross-eyed stereo photography. That's a completely different geometry than what a headset expects.

- **Raw**: We hand the HMD each eye's image exactly as the game rendered it (converged). The headset displays them assuming parallel-axis geometry. Since the actual camera angles don't match that assumption, objects don't line up at any consistent depth — hence "each eye looks correct individually, but they don't overlap," i.e. real double vision.
- **Symmetric**: We force the *math* (FOV bounds) to be parallel/symmetric and crop each eye's texture to compensate for the reported difference in FOV — but the pixels themselves are still the product of the original toe-in cameras. Cropping the UV rect doesn't undo the fact the content was rendered from an angled viewpoint. That's why symmetric "snaps" the framing closer together (less obviously double) but you still perceived a residual zoom/mismatch — the crop is fighting geometry it can't actually fix.

## What a real fix requires

To truly fix it, we'd need to take each eye's rendered image and **re-project/shear it** — essentially a horizontal keystone/shear transform per eye — to approximate what the image would have looked like from a parallel-axis camera at the same position. This is a post-process warp (shader pass) applied to the scene-capture/game texture before compositing to the swapchain, using the known toe-in angle (which we can derive from the logged raw FOV asymmetry, e.g. `~0.169` radians difference between `1.264` and `0.895`... actually the per-eye center offset) to compute a horizontal shear/perspective correction matrix.

Caveats:
- It's an **approximation** (a 2D image-space shear can't perfectly reconstruct true 3D reprojection — objects at different depths would need different correction amounts, but we only have the flattened 2D output). It will help most in the mid-frame region and be less perfect at extreme edges or very close-up objects.
- Since the toe-in angle appears constant (same FOV values every frame), the shear amount is a fixed constant, computed once — not per-frame expensive.
- It's implemented as a shader pass (similar to your existing `render_srv_to_rtv` blit path), so it's a moderate amount of new code in `D3D12Component.cpp`/`D3D11Component.cpp` plus a small shader, not a one-line toggle.

Do you want me to proceed with implementing this shear-correction pass?

## What you just told me (and why it changes everything)

- Projection override (Raw / Mirrored / Symmetrical horizontal) changes how far apart the eyes look, but it does **not** remove the artifact — it's just "harder to notice." That already told us this isn't primarily a horizontal-convergence/toe-in problem.
- The decisive part: **in 2D screen mode, looking through just one eye of the headset at a time, you still see blurring/double-image** at the same animation-finish moments.

If 2D mode presents a single flat image (not a stereo pair) and a *single eye* looking at that *single image* sees doubling, then this cannot be a left/right eye mismatch, toe-in/convergence problem, or stereo-geometry issue at all. There is only one image being shown. A doubled/blurred single image means **two temporally- or spatially-offset versions of the same frame's content are visible at once within one texture** — i.e., this is a **ghosting/temporal artifact**, not a stereo artifact.

## Re-reading the whole investigation with that lens

Everything we ruled out is still validly ruled out, but for a different reason than we thought:

- **TAA/Lumen/DLSS/AA disabled, still happens** — consistent with ghosting, since in-game AA/upsampling reprojection wasn't the source anyway.
- **NSF on/off, same-pass on/off, still happens** — consistent, because NSF only affects whether left/right are rendered together or separately; it doesn't touch single-eye temporal content.
- **Screenshots never capture it** — very consistent with a *compositor-side or presentation-timing* ghost (e.g., an old frame and new frame both being scanned out/blended for one instant), which a screenshot of the game's own backbuffer would never see.
- **Correlates with animation/cutscene finish and camera transitions, and menu entry/exit** — these are exactly the moments where render targets get resized/reallocated (`Reallocating view target!`, `Pass1 view_rect changed`) and where the scene-capture texture lifecycle changes.
- **It appeared to get worse/more noticeable after the "fix" to keep the last-known-good scene-capture texture bound instead of resetting it** — this is the biggest new suspect. That change was designed to stop the right eye from *mirroring* the left eye by holding onto stale content. But holding a stale texture across a transition is exactly the mechanism that produces a double-exposure/ghost if the old and new frame content ever get composited together (e.g., a partial-copy race, or the "last known good" frame being shown for one extra frame while the new one is also partially blitted on top, or the destination texture not being fully overwritten before it's read for presentation).

## Leading hypothesis now

**Single-frame/single-texture ghosting caused by stale texture retention or reallocation timing**, most likely centered on:
1. The scene-capture texture retention logic in `D3D12Component.cpp` (added specifically to fix the old right-eye mirroring bug) — worth testing whether reverting to "reset on null" but instead **skip-copy-this-frame** (rather than force a copy of a stale texture) changes the artifact.
2. The view-target reallocation path in `FFakeStereoRenderingHook.cpp` — during `Reallocating view target!`, if the old and new textures are both alive briefly and something reads from the old one after part of the new frame has already been written, you'd get exactly a doubled/blurred single image.
3. Possibly the OpenXR swapchain image index handling during resize — if we submit an image whose acquire/release/wait-for-fence sequence overlaps a resize, the runtime could show a partially-updated buffer next to leftover content from the previous swapchain image.

## What we've actually tried (recap, corrected)
- Disabled unsafe same-pass override — real bug, real fix, unrelated to this artifact.
- NSF pose-sync toggle — targeted eye-desync, not applicable now.
- Depth-submission A/B test — no change, consistent with this not being compositor depth reprojection.
- Controller crash fix (`is_using_controllers` noinline + SEH) — real, unrelated but valuable stability fix.
- Scene-capture stale-texture retention change — **now a prime suspect for causing/worsening the ghost rather than fixing it**.
- Horizontal/vertical projection overrides — proven not to be the root cause (artifact persists in all modes, just harder to see).

## Recommended next steps
1. **Isolate temporal vs stereo**: with 2D screen mode active, add (or use existing) logging around exactly which texture pointer/generation is bound to the swapchain image at the moment the compositor is told to present, during an animation-finish transition. We want to know if two different texture generations' content are visible in the same presented frame.
2. **Re-test the scene-capture retention fix**: temporarily replace "keep last-known-good texture" with "skip this frame's copy entirely if source is null" (i.e., don't touch the destination at all rather than binding possibly-stale content), and see if the doubling reduces. This isolates whether that specific fix is the source.
3. **Check reallocation ordering**: log the exact frame index/timestamp when the old texture is released vs when the new texture's first full write completes, relative to when a present/end_frame call consumes it. A race here (present happening before the new texture is fully written, while the GPU is still flushing the old one) would produce exactly this symptom.
4. **Check Pimax runtime settings**: since this is Pimax Crystal + OpenXR, verify PiTool's own "Smart Smoothing"/motion smoothing/ASW-equivalent is fully disabled — HMD-side frame interpolation is a classic cause of an artifact that only appears in the headset, never in screenshots, and is worst during fast camera motion (animations/cutscenes), including in flat/2D presentation.

## What the log shows (14:44:05.4 – 14:44:07.4, ~2 seconds)

At `14:44:05.399` a scene-capture texture is freshly created and bound (`rt=16289c0100`, `generation=5`). Then, starting almost immediately and continuing for **the next ~2 full seconds without stopping**, the log repeats this exact cycle over and over, roughly every 10–20ms (i.e., nearly every single rendered frame):

1. `get_desired_number_of_views_hook` / `begin_render_viewfamily_real` call `create_scene_capture()` again
2. It gets **throttled** ("only Nms since last creation, cooldown=3000ms")
3. Immediately after, `D3D12Component.cpp:694` logs **"Scene capture RT went null while m_scene_capture_tex was bound"** — same generation (5), same stale pointer (`16289c0100`)
4. The renderer falls back to "keep last-known-good" and reuses that same frozen texture again
5. Repeat, hundreds of times in a row

So for roughly two seconds straight, the engine is invalidating the scene-capture render target on almost every frame, our throttle is correctly refusing to thrash-recreate it, but the practical effect is: **the right eye is frozen on one static captured frame while the left eye (`game_tex`) keeps updating live**, for the entire ~2 second window. That's exactly the kind of stereo mismatch that would look like blur/ghosting/double-vision, especially during an animation where the camera/pose is actively changing underneath a frozen right-eye image.

This is a different bug from the toe-in/shear theory and from a pure reallocation race — it's **the scene-capture actor itself being repeatedly torn down or its render target repeatedly invalidated by the game**, way faster than our 3-second recreate cooldown can track, so the right eye effectively stalls.

## Why this could also explain 2D-mode/single-eye symptoms

If 2D screen mode's presented image is derived from the same composited double-wide backbuffer (game_tex left half + scene_capture right half, as seen in the composite logs), then whichever half of that backbuffer feeds the 2D view could still show a transient artifact tied to this same left/right freeze mismatch, or the underlying cause (whatever is repeatedly invalidating the scene-capture actor every frame) may itself be a broader per-frame render-state churn that also disturbs the primary view — not just the VR-specific right eye.

1. A brand new scene-capture render target is created and bound (`rt=16289c0100`).

## What this means concretely

The root problem is **not** stereo geometry/toe-in. It's: something in the game repeatedly makes the scene-capture render target report as null (a real per-frame invalidation from the engine, not fabricated by us), and every time that happens for longer than an instant, our safety throttle (added to prevent a crash-inducing recreate-thrash loop) forces the right eye to sit frozen on a stale image for up to 3 full seconds while the left eye keeps moving live — producing exactly the double-image/blur sensation during animations.

To fix this properly we have two independent angles, and we can do both:
1. **Reduce the visible symptom**: when this stuck/null condition is detected, temporarily suppress the mismatch (e.g., mirror left→right or force same-pass) instead of freezing on a stale right eye, so it's at least not a jarring stereo split during the ~3s window.
2. **Find and fix the actual invalidation trigger**: identify exactly what's nulling the render target repeatedly (level-transition GC? actor destroy/respawn? something specific to `no_local_pawn`/exception-handler recovery?) so it doesn't need throttling workarounds at all.

## Root cause of the dump failure and fix

`hr=0x80070032` is `ERROR_NOT_SUPPORTED`. `SaveWICTextureToFile` only accepts a hardcoded list of concrete `DXGI_FORMAT`s from the resource's own description — but our render textures (`m_game_tex`/`m_scene_capture_tex`) are created as **typeless** resources (that's why `TextureContext::setup` takes separate RTV/SRV view formats), so the underlying resource format is something like `DXGI_FORMAT_B8G8R8A8_TYPELESS`, which isn't in that list and always fails, regardless of what's actually on screen.

**Fix:** switched to `DirectX::SaveDDSTextureToFile`, which writes the raw resource bytes directly without requiring a WIC pixel-format match, so it works with typeless resources unconditionally. Output files are now `glitch_dump_<timestamp>_left.dds` / `_right.dds`, written to the mod's persistent directory (same place your logs are: `%AppData%\Roaming\UnrealVRMod\Client-Win64-Shipping\`).

## Root cause: the "sync-pose" fix silently zeroes out stereo separation

Look at lines 9127-9128 and 9140-9141 in `FFakeStereoRenderingHook.cpp`. The `sync-pose` diagnostic feature (which you enabled specifically to combat eye desync) doesn't just sync **rotation** between Pass1 (left) and Pass2 (right) when they diverge — it **unconditionally overwrites the right eye's `view_location`/`local_view_d` with the left eye's location, every single Pass2 frame**, regardless of whether there was any actual divergence:
```cpp
*rot_d = hook_data.m_nsf_sync_pose_rotation_double;
*local_view_d = hook_data.m_nsf_sync_pose_location_double;   // <-- always overwritten
...
*view_rotation = hook_data.m_nsf_sync_pose_rotation;
*view_location = hook_data.m_nsf_sync_pose_location;          // <-- always overwritten
```

`view_location` is the per-eye camera position, which normally differs between the left and right eye by the stereo/IPD offset — that's literally what creates 3D depth/parallax. By forcing the right eye's position to be identical to the left eye's every frame this path runs, you get **near-zero parallax between the two eyes** — exactly what your two screenshots show: the "affected" frame has almost no positional disparity between the character's position in the left vs right half, while the "normal" frame (where this sync apparently didn't fire, e.g. cached frame count mismatch) shows correct parallax.

So the divergence-delta logging only checked **rotation** divergence (which is why you saw "no Pass2 divergence events") — but the location was being clobbered silently with no logging at all, hiding the real culprit.

## The fix

Only rotation actually needs to be kept consistent between passes to prevent orientation-based desync during animation; location must retain its per-eye stereo offset. I'll stop forcibly overwriting location.

## Summary

**Root cause confirmed**: The NSF "sync-pose" fix you enabled to combat eye desync was overwriting the right eye's `view_location`/`local_view_d` with the left eye's location every frame it fired (not just rotation). This collapsed the stereo positional offset (IPD) between the two eyes, producing near-zero parallax — visually indistinguishable from "double vision"/flat depth, exactly matching your two comparison screenshots (affected frame has ~no left/right positional disparity, normal frame has correct parallax).

This also explains why your earlier logs showed "no Pass2 rotation divergence" — the divergence check only ever covered rotation; the location clobbering had no logging at all, so it was invisible in the log-only diagnosis.

**Fix applied**: `src\mods\vr\FFakeStereoRenderingHook.cpp` (~line 9113-9143) — Pass2 now only has its **rotation** forced to match Pass1 (preventing genuine orientation-based desync during camera transitions), while **location is left untouched**, preserving correct per-eye stereo parallax at all times.

## Summary

**Root cause of the crash**: Not a rendering logic bug — a GPU TDR (`DXGI_ERROR_DEVICE_REMOVED` / `DEVICE_HUNG`). The log shows `create_scene_capture()` being invoked and throttled dozens of times within milliseconds during heavy level-streaming (map/cutscene transition), because the existing loading-guard is keyed off `is_engine_tick_stalled()`, which can flicker `false` for a single frame even mid-load. One call slipped through the 3-second frequency cooldown during that storm, triggering a full descriptor-heap recreation (`rtv_heap`/`srv_heap` reset + rebuild) and texture rebind on `m_scene_capture_tex`. The very next frame then took **3857ms** to render (logged in `FRAME PACING`), and the following `Present()` call hung for 7.6 seconds before failing with device-removed — classic TDR behavior when GPU work piles up during an already-struggling loading frame.

**Fix applied**: `src\mods\vr\FFakeStereoRenderingHook.cpp` — `create_scene_capture()` (called from both `begin_render_viewfamily_real` and `get_desired_number_of_views_hook`) now requires the engine tick to have been reported **non-stalled for 5 consecutive checks** before it's allowed to actually recreate any render resources, instead of just a fixed 3-second cooldown. Any single stall report immediately resets the counter. This closes the race where a one-frame tick flicker mid-level-transition let expensive GPU resource recreation slip in at the worst possible moment.

**Next step for you**: reproduce the same map/cutscene transition that crashed before and confirm it no longer crashes. If it still hangs, grab the new log — you should now see repeated `"create_scene_capture() deferred - waiting for engine tick to stabilize"` warnings during the transition instead of the resource recreation actually happening, which would tell us there's still another path bypassing this guard.

## Root cause found and fixed

**The "Sync Eye Pose During Camera Transitions" feature has never actually worked** since it was introduced. The guard required `hook_data.m_nsf_sync_pose_frame_count == g_frame_count` to apply the Pass2 sync, but `g_frame_count` is assigned from `vr->get_runtime()->internal_frame_count` — the HMD runtime's frame counter, which increments **once per eye submission**. So it always advances by exactly 2 between the Pass1 (left) call and the Pass2 (right) call within the very same engine render frame (confirmed in your log: `Pass2 frame=7297` vs cached `Pass1 frame=7295`, `7453` vs `7451`, etc. — 100% consistent, every single occurrence). The frame-count equality check was therefore permanently false, and the toggle silently did nothing this entire time, explaining why your earlier tests with the sync-pose fix "on" showed no measurable difference in the diagnostics.

## Fix applied

In `calculate_stereo_view_offset()` (`src\mods\vr\FFakeStereoRenderingHook.cpp`):
- Removed the frame-count equality requirement — Pass1 and Pass2 run synchronously back-to-back within the same `begin_render_viewfamily_real` call (confirmed by the immediate `std::swap(views[0], views[1])` and re-invocation of the render module), so `have_left` alone is sufficient.
- `have_left` is now cleared immediately after being consumed by Pass2, so a stale cached pose can never leak into some unrelated, non-adjacent Pass2-only call.
- Kept the `NSF-POSE-DIVERGE-SKIP` and `NSF-POSE-DIVERGE`/`-TRACE` diagnostics so we can now see real applied rotation-sync activity and (unapplied) position deltas.

This is a genuine fix, not just added diagnostics — please rebuild the DLL, test the same 3 skill animations again with the toggle on, and send the new log. This time you should actually see the sync applying (via `NSF-POSE-DIVERGE`/`-TRACE` lines with `rot_delta` values reflecting real corrections), which may meaningfully reduce or eliminate the residual snap you described, since the mitigation is finally active instead of being a no-op.

## What the log shows

During your right-stick camera rotation, Pass1 and Pass2 render from **two different world positions** roughly 5 units apart (`pass1_pos=(1600.02,-975.13,496.01)` vs `pass2_pos=(1599.62,-973.45,500.71)`), not just different rotations. Our fix only forces **rotation** to match (by design — we can't force position without collapsing IPD/parallax). So during fast rotation, the right eye still renders from a position ~5 units away from where the left eye rendered, every single frame pair, and that gap only closes once the stick stops moving — which matches your description exactly ("doubled until the camera stops").

This is very likely **not a bug you introduced with a "guard"** — it's the fundamental limitation of NSF: Pass1 and Pass2 are literally two sequential render calls into the same frame, and if the camera keeps moving between them (continuous stick input, unlike a discrete instant snap), there's always going to be some residual per-frame position gap. AFR mode has the same class of issue but caches rotation only, similarly.

## Answering your actual question — guards you could selectively disable to test

Here are the candidates that could plausibly add extra timing/latency between the Pass1/Pass2 calls (worth trying one at a time):

This confirms real candidates. Here's what I found and a clear plan to test:

## Guards/toggles that could plausibly cause exactly this "double vision while turning, clears when the camera stops" symptom

1. **"Null Pass2 View State" (`is_native_stereo_fix_null_pass2_view_state_enabled`)** — this is the strongest suspect. Every frame, it wipes the right eye's `FSceneViewState`, which holds **TAA history and occlusion data**. That means the right eye loses temporal anti-aliasing accumulation and re-renders "cold" every single frame, while the left eye keeps full TAA history. During camera rotation, TAA-less rendering is far more prone to ghosting/doubling on any moving edge, and it would resolve once the camera stops (TAA catches back up in a few still frames) — matching your exact description. **Try disabling this first.**

2. **"Right Eye Shadow Fix" (`is_native_stereo_fix_right_eye_shadows_enabled`)** — you already tested this and said no change, so we can rule it out, consistent with what you told me earlier.

3. **Sync Eye Pose (the fix we just made functional)** — now that it's actually applying, if it's making things feel *worse* rather than better during fast rotation, that would also be worth an A/B test, since forcing rotation sync only on Pass2 does still leave the ~5-unit positional gap we saw in the log, which could itself look like doubling.

## Suggested test order

Since you can toggle these live in the mod's ImGui menu without a rebuild:
1. Turn OFF "Null Pass2 View State" only, test right-stick rotation.
2. If no change, turn it back on and turn OFF "Sync Eye Pose During Camera Transitions" instead, test again.
3. Report back which (if either) changes the doubling during camera turns.

This lets us isolate the cause with zero rebuild/log-round-trip cost. Want me to also add a diagnostic log specifically timestamping when the Pass2 view-state null happens, so we can correlate it precisely against your marker presses in the next log if the toggle test doesn't fully explain it?

## Why "distant/blurring during animation/VFX/skills" is happening, based on the evidence

We've now proven, frame-by-frame, that during any period of continuous camera motion (right-stick turning, skill cams, cutscenes), the engine calls Pass1 (left) and Pass2 (right) at two **different moments** — the camera keeps moving in between those two calls. Our fix corrects the **rotation** difference, but the **position** (view_location) is still whatever the camera happened to be at by the time Pass2 ran — confirmed by your log showing `pass1_pos=(1600.02,-975.13,496.01)` vs `pass2_pos=(1599.62,-973.45,500.71)`, a real ~5-unit gap. Since this is a *raw world position offset* (not rotation), it looks exactly like doubled/split vision until the camera stops moving and the gap closes — this fully explains the visual symptom you're describing for turning, skills, and cutscenes alike; they're all "the camera moved between the two eye calls" cases.

## Why my earlier caution doesn't actually apply here — key distinction

I need to correct myself: the *old* broken code (from before this session) copied Pass1's **already IPD-offset final position** onto Pass2, which literally forced both eyes to the same final render position — zero parallax, flat image. That's a different bug than what we should do now.

Looking at the function order: our sync-pose cache (lines ~9099-9110) captures `view_location` **before** the per-eye IPD offset (`eye_separation`) is computed and subtracted further down (that math runs later, unconditionally, using `true_index` to pick the correct per-eye offset). So if we sync the **raw pre-offset camera position** from Pass1 onto Pass2 (not the final offset one), the existing per-eye `eye_separation` subtraction still runs afterward for Pass2 using `true_index=1`'s own IPD offset — parallax is preserved, only the underlying camera-jitter-between-passes is removed.

Extend the sync-pose Pass2 branch to also overwrite the raw `view_location`/`view_d` with the cached Pass1 raw position, **before** the IPD/eye_separation math runs (which it already does later in the same function, unconditionally). This directly targets the exact bug your log proved exists, without repeating the old mistake.

Your evidence in bug2.txt proved the remaining doubling isn't IPD collapse (eye_separation stayed healthy at 2.9000) — it's that Pass1 and Pass2 sample the camera at genuinely different *world positions* mid-motion (~5 unit deltas), because the animated camera moves between the two render calls within the same frame.

Good — that's a very important clarification, and the tree/foliage case is the key clue here. Let me lay out why I think this reframes the whole problem, and propose a concrete non-code-yet direction.

**Why the tree case is the Rosetta Stone**

Leaves swaying in one eye but frozen in the other (and which eye flips depending on NSF on/off) is structurally identical to what we're now seeing with VFX/skills: it's not a camera pose problem, and it's not a post-process (motion blur) problem — it's a **per-frame "already updated" dirty-flag / double-buffer exclusivity problem**. Unreal has several subsystems that assume "this primitive/particle/instance gets updated exactly once per frame" and cache or consume a dirty bit the first time they're touched:

- Foliage WPO (wind sway) instance data / GPU Scene primitive uniform buffer updates
- Niagara/particle system per-view render data (transform history, ribbon/trail interpolation)
- Possibly skinned mesh "previous frame" bone buffers (which we already suspected for VFX)

In true stereo (synced sequential/AFR), each eye is understood by the engine as a genuinely separate frame/submission, so these systems re-evaluate for both. In NSF, Pass1 and Pass2 are **the same FSceneViewFamily, submitted back-to-back within one engine frame** — which is exactly why some of these subsystems only fire on whichever pass "claims" the update first (usually Pass1/left), then flag it consumed, leaving Pass2/right reading stale/previous data. That matches "frozen right eye" with NSF on, and would also explain skill VFX/particle blur being eye-asymmetric rather than a blur filter issue (which is why disabling motion blur did nothing — you'd already ruled that out via CVar, good to have that confirmed).

This also explains why you concluded "the only fix is emulating AFR's approach" — because AFR structurally avoids the problem (two real per-eye submissions), while NSF's efficiency trick (single shared family) is exactly what creates the exclusivity.

**New direction: don't chase every double-buffered subsystem — make the symptom structurally impossible during the risk window instead**

Rather than hunting down each individual dirty-flag system (foliage WPO, Niagara, skin cache, etc. — proven to be a losing battle already), use your own idea: **dynamically/conditionally mirror the right eye from the left during exactly the windows where this class of bug can manifest**, instead of running NSF's true independent Pass2 during those windows.

Concretely:
- You already have a static "Mirror Right Eye" toggle (always-on monoscopic fallback) and a live divergence detector (the `NSF-POSE-DIVERGE` rot/pos delta logging) that already fires precisely during camera transitions/skills/cutscenes.
- Instead of applying pose-sync only, use that same detector as a trigger: when rot/pos delta exceeds threshold (or a VFX/skill flag if the game exposes one), temporarily force Pass2 to become a literal mirrored copy of Pass1's finished frame for a short hold window (the divergence window plus a few frames of hysteresis so it doesn't flicker in and out), then resume true independent NSF stereo once motion settles.

"AFR has zero VFX ghosting" while NSF has it, even with motion blur off, confirms this is structural to how NSF shares one `FSceneViewFamily`/render pass between eyes — not a post-process or pose-timing issue at all. That lines up with the foliage case exactly as I suspected. Let's talk strategy only, as requested.

**Why AFR has no ghosting and NSF does**

AFR literally re-runs the *entire* render pipeline per eye, once per real engine frame each — so every double-buffered/one-shot-per-frame subsystem (foliage WPO, Niagara per-view caches, likely GPU skin cache "previous pose" buffers) naturally gets a fresh, correct evaluation for both left and right, just on different frames. NSF's core efficiency trick — reusing one `FSceneViewFamily`/`FScene` and only swapping `views[0]`/`views[1]` — is precisely what breaks this: anything that marks itself "already processed this scene frame" now only fires once, and Pass2 (whichever eye that is) inherits Pass1's already-stale state instead of an independent update. This isn't fixable by chasing the individual CVars/subsystems (you already proved that with the tree case) because it's an architectural byproduct of NSF's one-pass-shared-family design, not a specific feature toggle.

**Why your mirror mode is broken today (for future reference, not fixing now)**

Skimming the code: `is_native_stereo_fix_mirror_enabled()` forces `destroy_scene_capture()` every frame and makes D3D12 fall back to `copy_right(backbuffer)` (copying the pre-existing 2D backbuffer into the right eye) instead of `copy_left_to_right`. That's suspicious for two reasons: (1) it's copying the *2D flat-game backbuffer* render, not literally "left eye's finished stereo frame," which could easily be a different exposure/tonemap path than the VR eye textures → explains the brightness shift; (2) if `destroy_scene_capture()` keeps tearing down state every single frame while mirror is on, some upstream code may be short-circuiting to "keep last-known-good" texture (the same "stale scene capture" fallback logic we built earlier for the black-screen bug) instead of actually refreshing — explaining the static frame. This tells us the current mirror path was never designed as a live per-frame passthrough; it was a boot/fallback path repurposed. Any future "temporarily mirror" idea needs a real live left→right copy each frame, not this path.

**New direction, given both of those findings**

Since NSF's core single-pass-family design is the root cause, and mirroring is unproven/currently broken, I'd propose reframing the goal: rather than trying to patch NSF's sharing bug or "borrow" AFR behavior only during risk windows (fragile, timing-based, and we just agreed we have no clean trigger), consider **making NSF force a second independent pass through the exact subsystems that are known to misbehave, without going all the way to full AFR**. Concretely: NSF already does construct Pass2 as a second real render module invocation (`begin_render_viewfamily_real` re-calls the render module after `std::swap(views[0], views[1])`) — so the render itself *is* running twice. The difference from AFR is only the shared `FScene`/frame-count state. So the actual lever is: identify the specific "already processed this FScene frame" gate(s) that Niagara/foliage/skin-cache check, and force-reset just those specific gates between Pass1 and Pass2 (not the CVars, not motion blur, not pose) — effectively simulating "this is a new frame" for exactly the animation/VFX-relevant systems, while leaving everything else (which works fine today) alone.

**What this actually tells us**

SS naturally gets two RHI frames (two real Present/frame-boundary cycles), so both eyes see a freshly-written buffer. NSF renders both eyes inside one RHI frame, so Pass2 always reads the same GPU buffer slot Pass1 already populated — a hardware/driver-level double-buffer, not anything walkable from CPU code. You're right that forcing a real RHI frame boundary mid-tick is architecturally just reimplementing SS's cost/instability inside NSF, which defeats NSF's entire purpose.

Good question — let's compare these directly, because the performance profiles are very different.

**Mirror mode vs. live NSF↔AFR/SS switching: performance comparison**

A properly-working mirror mode is actually **cheaper than NSF's normal stereo rendering**, not more expensive — because you'd skip rendering Pass2 entirely and just copy Pass1's already-finished frame into the right eye's texture slot (a GPU copy, same cost class as what's already happening today for the broken version, just sourced correctly). No second scene render, no view-family reallocation, no RHI frame boundary changes. This is a pure win perf-wise during the window it's active, and trivially safe to flip on/off every frame if needed, since it's just "which source do I blit from" — no engine-state transition at all.

Switching NSF↔AFR/SS live is a different category of risk. In this codebase specifically, `is_using_afr()` gates a lot of structurally different code paths (pose caching, `views.count` overrides, scene-capture actor lifecycle, `get_desired_number_of_views` behavior, CVar toggles like HZBOcclusion/instance-culling that are NSF-only). Flipping that mid-game likely forces: scene capture destroy/recreate, view-target reallocation (which we saw earlier already causes a visible stall on its own, per the "force reallocation instead of waiting the 5-frame debounce" fix), and probably a frame or more of transient bad/duplicate state while it settles — for something you'd be doing every time the camera merely turns fast. That's a bad trade for a multiple-times-per-minute event. So: **fixing mirror mode is very likely the lower-cost, lower-risk option** of the two, assuming we fix its actual bugs (wrong source backbuffer, and the static-frame issue) rather than reusing its current broken implementation.

**Your other idea — detecting actual cutscenes instead of using delta-based heuristics — is a strong direction, and better than what I'd proposed.** Delta-thresholding (rot/pos divergence) only detects that the camera moved a lot; it doesn't distinguish "player spun the camera fast" (where you still want real stereo depth) from "an actual cutscene/skill-cam VFX moment" (where mirroring only during the true animation event is much safer and less likely to cause visible flicker in/out during normal gameplay). Many UE games expose a real state for this — worth checking if Wuthering Waves does:
1. Find cutscene/cinematic mode detection :white_check_mark:
Good news: there's a real, cheap signal available that's much better than delta-heuristics, and it doesn't require any new engine-side work — just a property lookup using the same pattern already used elsewhere in this codebase (e.g. the existing `bUsePawnControlRotation` bool-property lookup via `find_property`/`set_value_in_object` in `FFakeStereoRenderingHook.cpp`).

**Two native signals worth checking, in order of reliability:**

1. **`APlayerController::bCinematicMode`** — a real UE bool property that's set true during sequencer/matinee cutscenes almost universally across UE games (including many gacha/action titles built on UE4/5 like this one likely is). It's not currently bound in this SDK, but binding it is trivial: same `find_property(L"bCinematicMode")` + cached `FBoolProperty*` + `get_value_in_object()` pattern already used for `bUsePawnControlRotation`. This is a true "is a cutscene playing right now" signal, not a movement heuristic — it wouldn't fire during fast player-controlled camera turns or combat skills, only genuine cutscenes.

2. **`APlayerCameraManager`'s view-target blend state** (`PendingViewTarget`/`BlendParams`/`bIsBlending` in UE's `FTViewTarget`) — this is what actually drives ability-cam snaps and cutscene transitions/blends, so it would also catch the skill-camera-shift case (not just scripted cutscenes), which `bCinematicMode` alone would miss. This requires locating the offset the same way other struct fields were resolved elsewhere in this codebase (offset-scan pattern used for `FSceneViewInitOptions`), a bit more work than a simple bool property but still no new architecture.

**Why this is strictly better than delta-thresholding for triggering mirror mode:** it's an actual state flag rather than an inferred "camera moved a lot" guess, so it won't misfire during ordinary fast player-driven camera turns (avoiding needless flicker into/out of mono mode during normal gameplay), and it activates before the visual pose divergence even happens rather than reactively after a delta is observed — meaning less/no lag between "cutscene starts" and "mirror kicks in."

**Recommended combined plan, given the performance comparison:**
- Fix mirror mode properly (correct source: composite the *actual finished VR left-eye texture*, not the flat 2D backbuffer; and make sure it's re-copied every frame instead of freezing on a stale bind) — this is the cheaper, safer mechanism.
- Trigger it using `bCinematicMode` (and/or camera blend state) instead of rot/pos deltas — this is the safer, more precise signal.
- Keep the existing pose-sync toggles as-is for ordinary gameplay; they still help outside of true cutscene/ability-cam windows.

## What I fixed

**Root cause of the broken/static mirror image** (`src/mods/vr/D3D12Component.cpp`): the mirror-fallback path was calling `m_openvr.copy_right(backbuffer.Get(), ...)`, but `copy_right()` assumes a **double-wide** source and crops out the *right half* of it (see `D3D12Component.hpp` line 129-142: `src_box.left = m_backbuffer_size[0] / 2`). In NSF mode, the backbuffer passed in here is a normal single-width game frame, not double-wide — so that box read garbage/out-of-bounds data, producing the static/overbright right eye you saw. The AFR code path a few lines below correctly uses `copy_left_to_right()` (copies the *whole* left-half-sized region) for its own mirror case — I changed the NSF mirror branch to do the same.

I also added:
- A `mirror_requested` flag (from `should_mirror_right_eye_this_frame()`) into the existing `[VR][DIAG] NSF right-eye source changed` log, so you can tell whether a mirror event is coming from the manual toggle / cinematic auto-mirror vs. just a transient scene-capture gap on boot.

## Root cause (confirmed by your log)

Your log is full of repeated, back-to-back:
```
[VR][DIAG] Scene capture RT went null while m_scene_capture_tex was bound ... keeping last-known-good scene capture texture until a new one is bound
```
firing continuously for the same generation (`generation=4`) at ~10ms intervals — this is happening **during the VFX skill animation**, not during a cutscene. That's why `bCinematicMode` never fired (correctly — it's not a Sequencer cutscene) and why the right eye froze on one frame while the left kept moving: our existing "keep the last-known-good texture" policy has **no time limit**, so once the scene-capture RT goes null and stays null for the whole VFX window, the right eye is stuck presenting that single stale frame indefinitely.

## Fix applied (`D3D12Component.cpp`)

Added a stall-duration threshold using the stall tracker that already existed (`report_scene_capture_stall_frame()` / `get_scene_capture_stall_duration_ms()`, which your earlier diagnostic infrastructure built):

- If the scene-capture RT has been null for **< 100ms**, keep riding out the stale texture as before (handles single-frame reallocation blips without triggering an unnecessary mirror-diplopia flash).
- If it's been null for **≥ 100ms** (sustained stall — matches your VFX skill case), `using_mirror` now becomes true and the right eye switches to a **live mirrored copy of the left eye** (via the same corrected `copy_left_to_right()` path from the earlier fix) instead of staying frozen.
- Diagnostic log now includes `stall_too_long` and `stall_ms` fields so you can confirm in the log exactly when/why the fallback engages.

This means during a VFX/skill window: right eye starts frozen for up to ~100ms (brief, likely imperceptible), then switches to a live (moving, correctly-exposed) mono mirror of the left eye instead of staying stuck — trading brief stereo-freeze for continuous motion, which should look far better than a static frame.

Please grab a fresh log during the same VFX skill and check for `stall_too_long=true` and `NSF mirror-right-eye copy` lines, and let me know if the right eye is now moving (even if flat/mono) instead of frozen during that window. **Why the Lua reset makes the artifact "much less noticeable":**

The Lua snippet doesn't blend anything — it detects a *hard camera cut* (position jump >30 units or forward-vector rotation >10°) and does a discrete, one-shot `ResetCutSceneCamOffset()`. Two things make that effective:

1. **It distinguishes cuts from continuous motion.** A real cutscene/skill-camera cut is a discontinuity — there's no "correct" intermediate pose between old and new camera, so any blending across it produces a visibly wrong in-between frame in one eye (a flash of double-vision). Snapping instantly avoids ever rendering that wrong intermediate.
2. **It only intervenes on large deltas.** Small continuous per-frame drift (VFX motion, skill animation) is left alone, so it doesn't fight the natural animation.

Our existing NSF sync-pose code was applying the *same* blend alpha uniformly to every divergence, including hard cuts — so on a real camera cut it would smear Pass2 toward Pass1 over multiple frames, and that smear is what read as the lingering blur/double-image, worse than what the Lua approach produces.

**Fix applied** in `FFakeStereoRenderingHook.cpp` (both the double- and single-precision NSF sync-pose branches): when the already-computed `rot_delta`/`pos_delta` exceed Lua-equivalent thresholds (10° / 30 units), we force `blend_alpha = 1.0` (an instant full snap) regardless of the user's configured blend slider; otherwise we keep using the configurable blend for small continuous divergence. This directly replicates the cut-vs-continuous distinction from the Lua script while preserving the existing blend behavior for VFX/animation motion.

**What changed:** the hard-cut check no longer uses a flat 10°/30-unit threshold. It now lives in `FFakeStereoRenderingHook::is_nsf_sync_pose_hard_cut()` (in `FFakeStereoRenderingHook.hpp`) and requires **both**:
