2. **Raised absolute floor** — even a genuine spike must also clear 25°/80 units as a safety net, so noise or small stutters can't trigger it just because the recent baseline happened to be very low.

Both the double- and single-precision NSF sync-pose branches in `FFakeStereoRenderingHook.cpp` now call this shared helper instead of the flat thresholds, so genuine camera cuts should still snap instantly while thumbstick-driven rotation stays on the blended path. Good diagnostic question — and no, it doesn't change the root cause, it actually **confirms** it.

**Why:** Pass1 (left) and Pass2 (right) are two separate render calls issued back-to-back within the same engine frame, but they aren't guaranteed to be capturing the *identical* camera state — if the underlying game-side transition (menu open, conversation view-target switch, FOV zoom) lands on the game thread in between those two calls, one eye renders the "before" state and the other renders the "after" state. **Which eye ends up being the old vs. new one is essentially a coin flip based on timing** — it depends on exactly when the transition's data mutation happens relative to the Pass1/Pass2 calls, not on any fixed "left always lags" or "right always lags" relationship. So seeing it flip sides (left zooms, right snaps back — as opposed to always being the same eye) is expected and consistent with the same divergence mechanism, not a separate bug.

One thing this new report does add though: **FOV/zoom is a different field than what we're currently syncing.** Our current fix (`m_nsf_sync_pose_rotation`/`location`) only syncs rotation (and optionally position) between Pass1/Pass2 — it does **not** sync FOV. So a "zoom" artifact specifically (as opposed to a rotational snap) is very likely FOV changing mid-frame between the two passes, uncorrected by the existing fix. That's a distinct, addressable gap: we'd need to cache Pass1's FOV the same way we cache rotation, and force/blend Pass2's FOV to match it, using the same hard-cut-vs-blend logic already built.

Yes — that consistency is actually an important clue and it does sharpen (not overturn) the diagnosis.

**Why "coin flip" was the wrong framing:** Pass1 (left) and Pass2 (right) always run in the *same fixed order* every single frame — Pass1 first, Pass2 second, within the same `begin_render_viewfamily_real` call. So which eye ends up "old" vs "new" for a **given transition type** isn't random at all — it's deterministic, based on exactly where in the game's per-frame logic that specific transition (menu open, conversation switch, skill animation) writes its camera data relative to that fixed Pass1→Pass2 order. Different transition types hook into different game-thread callbacks/update paths, so they can consistently land on different sides of that Pass1/Pass2 boundary — explaining why one transition type is always right-eye and another is always left-eye, without it being random per-occurrence.

**This does refine the fix, in one important way:** our current sync-pose correction is **asymmetric by construction** — it only ever forces/blends **Pass2 (right eye)** to match Pass1's cached rotation (and optionally position). It never corrects Pass1. So:

- For transition types where the mutation lands *before* Pass1 captures (both eyes should see "new" data, but if Pass1 itself is delayed a frame relative to the mutation, Pass2 gets force-synced back to Pass1's stale value) — this explains a **consistently right-eye** artifact, and it's plausibly *our own correction* re-introducing a lag on the right eye rather than the raw engine race itself.
- For transition types where the mutation lands *between* Pass1 and Pass2 (Pass1 renders old, Pass2 renders new) — our rotation sync would correctly force Pass2 back toward Pass1's old rotation, but since **we don't sync FOV**, if the "zoom" is FOV-driven rather than rotation-driven, it slips through uncorrected — landing on whichever eye's FOV update path is out of sync for that transition, which for menu opens you're seeing consistently on the left.

So: the fix path doesn't fundamentally change, but it confirms two concrete gaps worth closing — (1) FOV isn't currently part of the sync-pose cache at all, and (2) our correction being one-directional (right-only) could itself be the source of the right-eye-specific snap for certain transitions, rather than the underlying engine race. Given your token budget, want me to prioritize just adding FOV to the existing sync/hard-cut cache (cheap, reuses existing mechanism), or also make the correction bidirectional/symmetric?

## What this tells us

Our NSF sync-pose logic is built entirely around detecting/correcting a Pass1-vs-Pass2 **rotation/position** mismatch. But the log proves that during this session — including whatever menu-opening zoom event you experienced — Pass1 and Pass2 never actually diverged in position or rotation at all. So:

1. Sync-pose had nothing to correct (rightly reporting 0 delta), which is consistent with you saying the toggle made no difference to the zoom effect.
2. Yet your manual **Camera Freeze** (position+rotation) *did* fix it.

Those two facts together mean the "zoom" artifact is very likely **not** a Pass1/Pass2 pose-divergence problem at all — it's something that camera freeze incidentally also suppresses, but through a different mechanism than what our sync-pose targets. The two candidates I'd suspect:

- **FOV/projection matrix divergence**, not position/rotation. A "zoom" effect is literally a FOV or projection-matrix change. Our sync-pose code only copies rotation/location into `calculate_stereo_view_offset()` — it never touches the projection matrix or FOV. If the menu transition briefly changes camera FOV (e.g. UE's camera-manager blending FOV during `SetViewTargetWithBlend`) and the two eyes' render calls sample that changing FOV at slightly different moments/interpolation points, you'd get exactly a "zoom in one eye, snap in the other" artifact — while `rot_delta_deg`/`pos_delta` stay at 0 the whole time because those are unaffected.
- Camera Freeze in the debug UI probably freezes the *entire* camera manager state (including FOV) rather than just feeding a cached pose into the stereo offset calc, so it masks this FOV path too — while our sync-pose fix doesn't.

## Suggested next step

Before touching more render code, I'd add a parallel `fov_delta`/projection-matrix divergence log next to the existing pose-divergence trace (same place, ~line 9258), so we can directly confirm whether FOV is what's actually moving between Pass1 and Pass2 during the menu-open/conversation-camera-switch moments. Good question — let's separate "what NSF fundamentally is" from "what could be fixed at a different layer."

## Why there are always 2 distinct FSceneViews

Looking at `begin_render_viewfamily_real` (line ~7011 onward): the engine constructs `views.count > 1` (both eyes) as normal for a native-stereo render. NSF then **deliberately** truncates `views.count = 1`, sets `wants_swap = true`, renders the left eye alone through the normal single-view render module call, then swaps `views[0]`/`views[1]` and re-invokes the render module a **second time** for the right eye. That's not a side effect — it's the entire mechanism NSF uses to get correct single-eye rendering without instanced stereo. Two separate `FSceneView` render passes, each fully independent, is the whole design. There's no way to "alternate" this into a single FSceneView without discarding the technique entirely.

## The actual "no two-PRIMARY-views" fix exists — it's UE's native Instanced Stereo Rendering

What you're describing — one pass, no duplicate `FSceneView`, no PRIMARY conflict — is exactly what Unreal's built-in **Instanced Stereo Rendering** (`vr.InstancedStereo`) does: both eyes share **one** `FSceneViewFamily`, one draw call per mesh with GPU instancing (`SV_ViewID`/`INSTANCED_STEREO` shader permutation) selecting the eye, so there's structurally only one "primary" view ever. That cvar reference is literally why `FSceneView.cpp`'s constructor-finder is scanning for `vr.InstancedStereo` string refs in the engine binary (line 131-193) — it's fingerprinting the constructor, not using the feature.

The reason NSF/this whole hook framework exists at all is that Wuthering Waves's shipped engine build has its native VR/stereo path stripped or non-functional (no HMD device attached at the engine level), so UEVR has to fake stereo rendering by hooking `FFakeStereoRendering` and manually driving two sequential mono passes. Instanced Stereo requires:

1. Shaders compiled with the `INSTANCED_STEREO` permutation for every material actually used in-game (this is baked at cook/shader-compile time — can't be toggled at runtime if the shipped shaders don't have that permutation).
2. The renderer's `IStereoRendering` interface reporting instanced-stereo support and view count semantics consistent with it — currently `FFakeStereoRendering` is a synthetic stand-in that doesn't implement that path.

If the shipped game's shaders don't include the instanced-stereo permutation (likely, since it's a mobile/PC hybrid title not built with native PCVR support), turning on `vr.InstancedStereo` wouldn't unify the two views — it would just break rendering (missing shader permutation = fallback/pink/black materials), which is a very plausible **second, separate reason** black-screens tend to happen whenever "true single-pass" is attempted here.

## Bottom line

- No safe alternation trick avoids two `FSceneView`s — it's inherent to NSF.
- The "real" single-pass fix is UE's native Instanced Stereo, but it depends on shader permutations baked at cook time that this game very likely never compiled, so forcing it via cvar/engine-code patch is a much bigger and riskier investigation (would need to verify shader permutation availability first, which isn't something we can safely probe from outside the engine without a lot of new instrumentation).
- Given the same-pass PRIMARY/PRIMARY test just proved black-screen-both-eyes with zero exceptions, I'd treat "single shared pass" as **not viable** for this game build without that deeper shader-level verification, and keep focusing on the projection/FOV divergence lead instead, since that's fixable within the existing two-pass architecture.

Want me to look into whether there's any log/engine evidence of instanced-stereo shader support before ruling it out completely, or hold off and focus on your NSF-PROJ-DIVERGE test results?

I found the exact structural source of the per-frame lag you're asking about.

## Root cause: real wall-clock time elapses between Pass1 and Pass2 renders

Looking at `begin_render_viewfamily_real` (lines 6966-7389):

1. **Pass1 (left eye)** is fully rendered first — line 7159: `m_render_module_begin_render_viewfamily_hook.unsafe_call(...)`. This is a **synchronous, blocking** call into the engine's real render-module function that does the actual GPU command generation for the left eye. This can take real CPU time (several ms), especially during heavy VFX/animation-driven camera frames.
2. Only **after** that full call returns does the code swap views (`std::swap(views[0], views[1])`, line 7220) and prepare Pass2 (right eye).
3. Pass2 then gets rendered via the **same** `unsafe_call` a second time (line 7389 area).
4. The camera pose used for each `FSceneView` construction (in `calculate_stereo_view_offset`, where your `NSF-POSE-DIVERGE` trace lives) is sampled **fresh from the live, ticking camera actor** at the moment each pass's `FSceneView` is constructed — not cached from a single frame snapshot.

So the sequence per engine frame is actually:
```
sample camera pose -> construct Pass1 FSceneView -> render Pass1 (blocking, N ms) -> 
sample camera pose AGAIN (now N ms later, actor has moved) -> construct Pass2 FSceneView -> render Pass2
```

During continuous motion (dashing/running), the game's camera-actor tick keeps advancing between step 1 and step 2 above, because nothing pauses the live actor/animation state just because you're mid-render. That's exactly why your glitch markers all land inside sustained `NSF-POSE-DIVERGE` runs (~0.1-0.3°, ~2-5 units) that scale with how much camera velocity there is — it's proportional to **elapsed real time × camera angular/linear velocity**, not a discrete "cut."

Your existing sync-pose fix (forcing Pass2's rotation to match Pass1's cached rotation) already correctly compensates for this specific effect for **rotation**. It intentionally leaves **position** untouched because position legitimately carries per-eye IPD offset — but that means the *actor-movement* component of position drift (not the IPD-based stereo offset) is currently uncompensated, which is exactly what `pos_delta` in your log is measuring.

## Proposed fix

Instead of trying to derive "IPD-only" delta from raw position, cache Pass1's location **and** apply only the *difference* between Pass2's naturally-computed IPD offset and Pass1's, i.e.:

Right eye position = Pass1 cached actor position + (Pass2's own position − Pass2's own position projected without stereo offset)

Practically, the cleanest fix: capture the camera's base (non-stereo-offset) actor pose once before Pass1 renders, and force **both** Pass1 and Pass2 to compute their view offset from that single frozen base pose, applying each eye's own IPD offset relative to it — instead of letting each pass re-derive the base pose from the live (possibly-moved) actor.

Do you want me to implement this — i.e., snapshot the base actor pose once per frame (before Pass1's `FSceneView` construction) and have both `calculate_stereo_view_offset` calls derive their eye offset from that single snapshot rather than re-sampling the live actor for Pass2?

No — the original 6-frame version would **not** have captured your ~1 second glitch. At 90 FPS, 6 frames is only ~66ms, less than 7% of the event. I've now fixed it:

## :speech_balloon: GitHub Copilot
1. Read FFakeStereoRenderingHook.cpp, lines 9078-9160 :white_check_mark:
Good question — this is worth explaining clearly since it changes what we should investigate next.

**What the "block extra view" experiment actually did**

The hypothesis was: for this game, `calculate_stereo_view_offset()` gets called more than twice per frame (view_index sequences like 0,1,2,3...), and any call beyond the real left/right pair was assumed to be a *secondary* view — e.g. a VFX/portal material's own internal scene-capture stereo pass reusing the same hook. The "block" toggle made the code treat calls outside a computed "main stereo pass" range as not-a-real-eye, and skip applying VR pose/offset work to them entirely (early return, leaving the engine's own transform untouched).

**Why that broke the right eye (stuck to HMD)**

When you enabled the block, the right eye stopped following the game's actual per-eye offset logic and instead just passed through whatever the engine's raw (non-VR) transform was for that call — which is essentially "camera + your literal HMD pose" with no independent per-eye IPD offset math applied. That's why it visually "stuck to the HMD": we weren't blocking a *decorative* extra pass, we were blocking **the real right-eye call itself**, so it degraded to unmodified head tracking instead of proper stereo offset.

**Why that also caused the permanent doubled view**

The matching restriction in `calculate_stereo_projection_matrix()` used the *same flawed view_index classification* to decide when to call `update_matrices()`/apply the VR projection override. Since the classification was wrong, one of the two real per-frame projection calls was being skipped unconditionally — meaning one eye kept an unfixed/mismatched projection matrix on every single frame, regardless of the toggle's on/off state (the "off" path still had the incorrectly-gated projection logic in place; only the view-offset block was actually toggleable). That's the permanently doubled image you saw with the toggle both on and off.

**Is this actionable for the real fix?**

## What this gives you

A new toggle: **"DIAG: Log Final Per-Eye Camera Pose (spammy)"** (right under the skin-cache toggle in the UEVR menu).

Unlike everything logged so far (which only compared Pass1-vs-Pass2 pose *within the same frame*, or only fired during a short glitch-marker capture window), this logs the **fully resolved final camera position + rotation for each eye, every single frame, continuously** — tagged `[VR][NSF-FINAL-EYE-POSE] eye=0/1 frame=... pos=(x,y,z) rot=(pitch,yaw,roll)`.

This is exactly the diagnostic you're asking for: "how does the camera move with each eye, does it differ, is there an offset, where does it go." Because it's not gated to a 250ms/3s window, you can:

2. Reproduce the glitch (finish a skill animation, open a UI menu).
3. Disable the toggle again.

## What to look for in the log

- If **eye=1's** `pos`/`rot` values visibly creep/interpolate toward `eye=0`'s values over several consecutive frames while `eye=0` already sits at the final value — that proves one eye's camera value is lagging via an actual interpolation/lerp, confirming your "one eye slowly zooms while other snaps" observation is a real per-eye pose difference, not a rendering artifact.
- If **both eyes' values already match every frame** during the glitch, then the camera pose itself is fine and the issue is downstream (composite/mirror timing, TAA/temporal reprojection, or scene-capture texture staleness) — meaning we should stop looking at pose code and pivot to the D3D12 compositing/reprojection path instead.

This should let one capture settle the question definitively, rather than more speculative fixes.

## New toggles in the VR menu

1. **"DIAG: Log Final Per-Eye Camera Pose"** log line now also includes `view_index=` (in addition to `eye=`), so future captures will clearly show all 3 calls per frame instead of hiding the 3rd one under `eye=0`.

Here `view_index=3` is cleanly alternating 1:1 with `view_index=2`, tracking a completely normal, correctly-diverging stereo pair (left/right positions differing by a consistent, stable IPD-like offset every frame, not slowly converging). That matches exactly what you observed empirically:

- Suppress `2` → left eye follows HMD (same thing, mirrored — you blocked the *real right eye*).
- Suppress `1`, `0`, `4` → no visible change at all, meaning those indices are either never hit in this session, or are truly-inert secondary calls (portrait/minimap/etc.) that don't affect the main view.

## Root cause reassessment

`view_index` is **not a stable, absolute eye identifier** — it's runtime-order-dependent. The code's own `index_starts_from_one` / `index_was_ever_two` flags (which I saw in `FFakeStereoRenderingHook.cpp` around line 9024) exist specifically because Unreal doesn't guarantee a fixed numbering; the mapping from raw `view_index` to logical left/right (`true_index`) is inferred heuristically from the *sequence* of values seen so far. That heuristic can clearly assign a different physical `view_index` to "left eye" across separate play sessions (or even within one, if a capture/portrait view perturbs the sequence in between).

So the earlier "third call slowly converging toward the real eye" observation almost certainly wasn't a fixed extra `view_index=3` call — it was two real per-eye calls plus a **third, less frequent call whose `view_index` value shifts depending on session state**, and my fix mistakenly hardcoded index `3` from one capture as if it were a universal constant.

## What this means going forward

Blocking by raw `view_index` number is unreliable and dangerous (as you found — it can knock out a real eye). We need a way to identify the "extra" call that isn't tied to the raw index value itself. Good candidates, using signals already present in the codebase:
- The `is_full_pass` flag and `index_was_ever_two`/`index_was_ever_negative` state — logging these alongside `view_index` would show which of the 3 calls is the odd one out structurally, not numerically.
- Correlating with a scene-capture/render-target pointer (as was explored for the minimap/portrait capture hypothesis) — if the "extra" call shares a render target with a known secondary capture, that's a much safer signal to filter on than a bare index.

I'd suggest reverting reliance on the hardcoded suppress-by-index approach as a "fix" (keep the toggle as a diagnostic only, default off, and don't recommend index 3 anymore) and instead add one more diagnostic pass that logs `is_full_pass`, `index_was_ever_two`, and ideally the render-target/view-family pointer next to each `NSF-FINAL-EYE-POSE` line, so we can identify the extra call by a structural property instead of a session-dependent number. **Why native stereo (without the fix) is exposed too:**

The `vr->set_world_to_meters(world_to_meters)` call — and now the new `NSF-WTM-VALUE`/`NSF-WTM-MISMATCH` diagnostic — sits right at the top of `calculate_stereo_view_offset()`, **before** any `is_native_stereo_fix_enabled()` branching happens later in the function. This function is the engine's real `CalculateStereoViewOffset` hook — it gets called for **every** view/eye regardless of whether NSF is on or off. NSF only changes what happens *after* this point (pose sync, true_index aliasing logic, same-pass handling, etc.). The `true_index` parity computation itself (`index_starts_from_one`/`view_index % 2`) also runs unconditionally, so if the engine really is supplying a different `world_to_meters` per eye call, that would corrupt eye-offset scaling whether NSF is active or not. Native stereo without the fix just means you lose NSF's compensating pose-sync/aliasing mitigations — it doesn't mean this earlier code path is skipped.

So: **enable the two new diagnostics regardless of your NSF toggle state** when reproducing native-stereo doubling, and the same `NSF-WTM-MISMATCH`/`NSF-TRUE-INDEX-ALIAS` logs will tell you if it's the same root cause there too.

**"2D mode" doubling is a different question:**

If by "2D mode" you mean non-stereo/flat rendering (single view, no HMD stereo pass), then `calculate_stereo_view_offset` shouldn't be getting called with two competing indices at all in that path — a doubled image there is more likely a compositing/mirror issue (e.g., `D3D12Component.cpp`'s mirror-fallback path, or a stale/duplicated render target) rather than the `true_index`/world-scale aliasing we've been chasing, since aliasing requires the engine to be issuing multiple per-eye stereo calls in the first place.

## What we can now rule out (given 2D-mode/native-stereo/NSF all show it)

- **Eye-pairing/offset math** — ruled out. `is_2d_screen` guard proves head_offset/eye_separation is completely skipped in 2D mode, yet you still see it there. Whatever's happening is single-view-compatible.

## New leading candidate: TAA / temporal reprojection artifacts from camera-pose jitter

This is the one mechanism that is **single-view-compatible** and explains your described symptom exactly — "blurs, then resolves back to a single sharp image over about a second" is the textbook signature of **Unreal's Temporal Anti-Aliasing (TAA) history buffer rejecting/re-converging** after a sudden camera pose discontinuity. TAA accumulates multiple past frames using each frame's `PrevViewProjectionMatrix`; if the camera position/rotation this hook writes into `view_location`/`view_rotation` jumps or is inconsistent frame-to-frame (exactly what we're forcing here via the live `vr->get_rotation(0)`/`get_position(0)` reads plus your camera_forward/right/up offsets, applied **unconditionally on every call**, in every mode), the TAA history becomes momentarily invalid, producing exactly the "double image slowly resolving to single" look you're describing — and it would appear in 2D mode too, because TAA operates per-view regardless of stereo/NSF/AFR.

Given this, the most productive next diagnostic isn't more log analysis of eye-pairing — it's testing whether **disabling TAA temporarily** (or forcing `r.TemporalAA.Upsampling`/`r.DefaultFeature.AntiAliasing` off, or setting `r.TemporalAACurrentFrameWeight 1` to zero history blending) makes the blur-then-resolve artifact disappear. During camera transitions (skill/animation end, menu open/close, UI return), the two rendered views desync: one camera **snaps** to the new position instantly while the other **zooms/lerps back slowly** over ~1 second, producing a doubled/blurred image that gradually re-converges into clean stereo. ## Ruled out (with evidence)

| Hypothesis | How it was disproven |
|---|---|
| Mirror-path compositing bug | Fixed early on (`D3D12Component.cpp` mirror source); symptom persisted |
| Same-stereo-pass (force both PRIMARY) | Caused black screen both eyes — rejected |

| Leftover UI-quad scene-capture actor | Code audit: only one spawn site exists (`create_scene_capture()`); your UI-quad work used the OpenXR overlay, never touched the world |

## Most likely candidate (strongly supported)

**The scene-capture camera's pose lags the main game camera during camera-blend transitions.** Key structural discovery: in 2D Screen Mode the compositor literally blits `m_game_tex` (main camera) on the left half and `m_scene_capture_tex` (the NSF scene-capture camera) on the right half — so what you saw in 2D mode was the **same two-camera desync displayed side-by-side**. This explains all three affected modes with one mechanism, and explains why AFR/synced-sequential are immune (they alternate a single camera instead of running two live cameras).

The likely specific mechanism: the game's camera-blend (Unreal `SetViewTargetWithBlend`-style interpolation at animation/menu end) updates the main camera's pose, but the scene-capture camera receives its pose through `calculate_stereo_view_offset` calls keyed off parity-derived `true_index` — and the sync-pose logic's hard-cut/blend-alpha gating isn't fully closing the gap during the blend window, so one camera follows the blend while the other snaps (or vice-versa).

Excellent — that confirms the fix. Here's the full technical explanation of what was happening and why excluding `view_index=1` fixed it.

## The mechanism: how NSF's sync-pose cache works

Your mod's "Native Stereo Fix" (NSF) renders both eyes within the **same engine frame**, not across two alternating frames like AFR (Alternate-Frame Rendering). It does this via two back-to-back calls into `calculate_stereo_view_offset()` (Pass1 = left eye, Pass2 = right eye), triggered by a `std::swap(views[0], views[1])` and re-invocation inside `begin_render_viewfamily_real`.

Because the two eyes are built microseconds apart from *live* camera state, if the animated camera (dash, ability, cutscene blend) moves between the Pass1 call and the Pass2 call, the two eyes get built from two **different poses** — a momentary left/right rotation mismatch, perceived as "blurring"/double vision. To fix that, the code added a one-frame cache:

- Pass1 (`true_index == 0`, left) runs first and caches its rotation/location into `hook_data.m_nsf_sync_pose_*`, sets `have_left = true`.
- Pass2 (`true_index == 1`, right) reads that cached pose and **force-overwrites its own rotation** with Pass1's, then clears `have_left`. Only rotation is forced — position is deliberately left alone because it legitimately differs between eyes (IPD offset).

This mechanism is correct in principle — as long as `true_index` reliably alternates 0/1 exactly twice per frame, once per real eye.

## The bug: a third call was polluting `true_index`

`true_index` isn't derived from a real "which eye is this" engine flag — it's derived purely from `view_index`'s **parity** (even/odd). Your `NSF-RAW-VIEW-INDEX` logging proved the engine actually calls `calculate_stereo_view_offset()` up to **three times per frame** with raw `view_index` values of `1`, `2`, and `3` — not just two. Because `true_index` only cares about parity:

- `view_index=2` → `true_index=1` (odd... actually even→ maps differently, but empirically this was the real right eye)
- `view_index=3` → `true_index=0`
- `view_index=1` → **also** `true_index=0`

So `view_index=1` and `view_index=3` were **aliasing onto the same `true_index=0` slot** — both treated as "Pass1/left" by the cache logic. `NSF-TRUE-INDEX-ALIAS` logging directly caught this collision happening ~33,000 times in your capture.

## Why this produced blurring, and why it flipped eyes across sessions

Since both `view_index=1` and `view_index=3` write into the *same* `m_nsf_sync_pose_*` cache slot as "the left pose," whichever of the two calls happened to fire **last** before the real Pass2 (right eye) read the cache would win the race:

- If the real left-eye call (`view_index=3`) wrote last → cache was correct → no visible issue that frame.
- If the extra, non-visual call (`view_index=1`) wrote *after* the real left eye and *overwrote* the cache with its own (irrelevant/stale/non-eye) pose → Pass2 then force-applied that wrong rotation onto the real right eye → an instant, wrong rotational snap on one eye only → read as blur/double-vision for that frame.

Because this was a **timing race between three interleaved calls**, not a fixed ordering, it explains why you sometimes saw the glitch on the left eye and sometimes the right — whichever eye happened to read the polluted cache that frame took the visible hit.

Your earlier direct test (fully early-returning `view_index=1` before any caching/rendering) proved no eye went stuck/blank/frozen — confirming `view_index=1` isn't a real displayed eye at all; it's a redundant/internal call (likely a shadow-depth pass, occlusion query, or other internal `CalculateStereoViewOffset` invocation UE issues that never reaches a composited viewport).

## The actual fix

Rather than fully skip rendering `view_index=1` (which felt riskier — some other subsystem might still depend on it running), I added a narrower guard:
```cpp
const bool diag_exclude_from_sync_cache = vr->is_diag_exclude_view_index_from_sync_cache_enabled() &&
    view_index == vr->get_diag_exclude_view_index_from_sync_cache();

if (!diag_exclude_from_sync_cache && vr->is_native_stereo_fix_enabled() && ...) {
    // sync-pose cache read/write happens here
}
```

With the toggle enabled and index set to `1`, that specific call is simply never allowed to touch `m_nsf_sync_pose_*` at all — it can no longer win the race and overwrite the real left eye's cached pose. The real `view_index=2`/`3` (right/left) calls are completely untouched, so real stereo pose-sync behavior is preserved, but the polluting third call is removed from the equation. That's exactly what eliminated the blur in your latest log with no other regressions.

Great data points — let's unpack each one, because they actually point to two **separate, independent** mechanisms in the code, not one bug needing "two fixes" by accident.

## 1. Why the sync-pose toggle being off makes the index-exclusion do nothing

Look at the exact gating on the cache block:
```cpp
const bool diag_exclude_from_sync_cache = vr->is_diag_exclude_view_index_from_sync_cache_enabled() &&
    view_index == vr->get_diag_exclude_view_index_from_sync_cache();

if (!diag_exclude_from_sync_cache && vr->is_native_stereo_fix_enabled() && !vr->is_using_afr()
    && vr->is_native_stereo_fix_sync_pose_enabled() && !is_full_pass) {
    // ...entire cache read/write + blend/snap logic lives in here...
}
```

The exclusion flag only decides whether `view_index==1` is allowed to **enter** this block. But the whole block — cache, hard-cut detection, blend, snap — is **also** gated on `is_native_stereo_fix_sync_pose_enabled()`. If that main toggle is off, the block never runs *at all*, for any index, so there's nothing for the exclusion to protect against — the cache-pollution bug and its fix both live inside a feature that has to be turned on first. That's expected, not a bug: you need **both** `NativeStereoFixSyncPose` (the feature) **and** `DiagExcludeViewIndexFromSyncCache` (the guard against index=1 corrupting it) enabled together.

## 2. Only index=1 causing it — consistent with the evidence

Good confirmation. This matches the `NSF-TRUE-INDEX-ALIAS` log data exactly: `view_index=1` and `view_index=3` are the two values that collide on `true_index=0`. Excluding `2` or `3` instead removes a **real eye's** contribution from the cache, so of course the corruption/race reappears (now the real left-eye pose itself is missing every other frame, reintroducing exactly the same kind of divergence).

## 3. The "snap in both eyes instantly" vs "converge naturally over ~1s" issue

This is a **completely separate mechanism** from the index-1 exclusion — it's the hard-cut/blend logic just below the cache write:
```cpp
const bool is_hard_cut = hook_data.is_nsf_sync_pose_hard_cut((float)rot_delta, (float)pos_delta);
...
const auto blend_alpha = (is_hard_cut || force_full)
    ? 1.0
    : (double)vr->get_native_stereo_fix_sync_pose_blend_alpha();

if (blend_alpha >= 1.0) {
    *rot_d = hook_data.m_nsf_sync_pose_rotation_double;   // full instant snap
} else if (blend_alpha > 0.0) {
    rot_d->yaw = std::lerp(rot_d->yaw, hook_data.m_nsf_sync_pose_rotation_double.yaw, blend_alpha); // gradual
    ...
}
```

Two important facts about this:
- **This logic only ever touches Pass2 (the right eye).** The left eye (`true_index==0`, Pass1) is always treated as ground truth and is never modified. So structurally, "both eyes converge" isn't currently possible — only the right eye is ever pulled toward the left, never the reverse. That's why you noticed "one eye did not seem to be doing that before" — before the index-1 fix, the *cache itself* was sometimes corrupted (holding index-1's irrelevant pose instead of the real left eye's), so the right eye would sometimes snap to garbage instead of to the real left pose. Now that the cache is clean, the snap target is always correct — hence "less blur" — but it's still an instant, one-frame, one-eye-only snap whenever `is_hard_cut` is true, not a gradual multi-frame convergence.
- **`blend_alpha` is only gradual when `is_hard_cut` is false.** Whenever a hard cut is detected (large sudden delta), the code deliberately forces `blend_alpha = 1.0`, bypassing the smooth slider entirely, on the reasoning that blending across a genuine cut would show a visibly-wrong intermediate frame. That's why you're seeing instant snaps rather than a ~1-second convergence.

## Why *any* gradual blend amount breaks it (not just full snap)

Look at what `calculate_stereo_view_offset()` actually controls: it only mutates `view_rotation`/`view_location` — the values later used to build **this view's projection/culling frustum** for that render pass. UE's per-view frustum culling (which decides what foliage/tree/mesh instances are visible, including HLOD/Nanite/occlusion culling with per-frame hysteresis) is derived from the **exact, complete** rotation passed out of this function — it's captured as a coherent snapshot immediately afterward, not something UE re-derives gradually.

- **Full snap (`blend_alpha=1.0`)**: Pass2's rotation becomes *exactly* Pass1's rotation. The resulting frustum is fully self-consistent — it matches a rotation the engine has genuinely seen before (Pass1's), so all downstream culling/occlusion/HLOD systems treat it as a valid, coherent camera state.
- **Any partial blend**: Pass2's rotation becomes a **synthetic value that was never a real camera pose** — not Pass1's, not Pass2's original, not anything the culling/occlusion hysteresis system has valid cached state for. Many of UE's visibility systems (tree/foliage culling especially) use frame-over-frame hysteresis and bounding-margin logic that assumes continuity between real poses — feeding it a one-off interpolated value breaks that continuity and produces exactly the kind of asymmetric, per-eye culling glitch you're describing (tree culling correct in one eye, wrong in the other).

That also directly explains your observation that tree culling **flips L/R** when NSF is off — this isn't a bug you introduced with the pose-sync fix; it's inherent to **each eye computing its own independent frustum/culling pass** from its own `view_index`'s pose sample, and whichever underlying raw call currently maps to which eye determines which eye's culling data is "fresh" vs "stale" at any given moment.

All of these reuse `IStereoRendering::CalculateStereoViewOffset` to get a stereo-correct camera pose for their sub-view, but build their own lightweight view struct (e.g. `FProjectedShadowInfo`/`FViewMatrices`) instead of allocating a full top-level `FSceneView`.

3. **It aliases to `true_index=0`**, same bucket as the real left/eye-A view (index 3 also → true_index 0). That's a coincidence of the parity math, not evidence it's a real second eye — it's just why our old cache-write logic corrupted the real eye-A pose cache.

**Conclusion: index 1 is very likely a shadow-cascade or occlusion/HZB sub-view pass**, not a discardable "garbage" call and not a third eye. That lines up exactly with your symptom: tree/foliage sway culling and shadows are driven by exactly these systems (shadow depth passes and occlusion culling use their own view/frustum derived from a `CalculateStereoViewOffset` call, separate from the final composited eye).

Excluding index 1 from the cache doesn't fix its pose — it just stops its (possibly-in-progress, mid-cascade) pose from **overwriting** the real eye's cached "last known good" pose. That's why blur/desync improved. But it does nothing to correct whatever pose is being handed *to* index 1 itself, so the shadow/culling subsystem it feeds keeps getting whatever raw (possibly stale, possibly mid-cascade) pose the engine computed for it — hence the culling/shadow inconsistency you're now seeing, which is a separate half of the same bug.

Instead of excluding index 1 from the sync system, feed it the **same corrected/synced pose being applied to the real eyes**, without writing its own result back into the shared cache. That should keep shadow/culling frustums coherent with the actual HMD pose (fixing the sway/culling glitches) while not polluting the eye-pose baseline (keeping the blur fix intact).

## :speech_balloon: GitHub Copilot
Good question — let me lay out why "let index 1 feed both eyes" is conceptually different from what excluding it currently does, and why it's riskier than it sounds.

## What the cache actually is right now

The sync-pose cache has exactly **two logical slots**, keyed by `true_index` (0 = left, 1 = right). The existing (working) fix does this:
- Pass1 (left, `true_index=0`) **writes** its rotation/position into the cache.
- Pass2 (right, `true_index=1`) **reads** that cache and snaps/blends its own rotation to match Pass1's.

So the real eyes *already* converge onto **one** shared pose per frame — that's the whole point of NSF sync. The blur/desync you originally had wasn't "the eyes never agree," it was "index 1 was **also** writing into that same shared slot, in between or after Pass1/Pass2, with a different pose" (since it aliases to `true_index=0`, the same slot Pass1 uses). Because index 1 fires a *variable* number of times per frame (2 to 9+ calls), it could stomp Pass1's correct cached pose with a stale/mid-cascade one right before Pass2 read it — that race is what caused the blur.

## Why "let it feed both eyes" doesn't mean what it sounds like

If you let index 1 write to the cache too, it isn't "feeding both eyes" as a *third* independent contribution — it's **competing for the same single write slot** Pass1 already uses. Whoever writes last wins, and since index 1's call count/timing relative to Pass1/Pass2 is not fixed, you get a non-deterministic pose selected each frame. That's exactly the bug, not a fix.

## What you're actually proposing (I think): make index 1 *authoritative* for both eyes

A different, legitimate idea: instead of Pass1(left) writing the cache and Pass2(right) reading it, have **index 1's last call each frame** be the thing that seeds the cache, and have **both** Pass1 and Pass2 snap/blend to *that* value. This is feasible to implement, but has real risks:

1. **Timing is unknown/unstable.** We don't yet know if index 1's calls always happen *before* both Pass1 and Pass2 in a frame, or interleaved between them. If it fires again *after* Pass1 but *before* Pass2, you'd correctly sync both eyes. If it fires only *before* both, you'd introduce a small lag (both eyes render from an older pose than the true current camera) — not a left/right split, but a whole-frame lag/judder during fast motion.

2. **It's likely not even a camera-eye pose.** Since index 1 appears structurally tied to a shadow-cascade/occlusion sub-view (per NSF-VIEWINDEX-IDENTITY: no `FSceneView`, variable per-frame call count), its rotation/position may be a legitimate camera-relative transform but computed for a shadow slice, not guaranteed identical to the actual eye camera framing. Forcing both real eyes onto it risks subtly wrong FOV/orientation feel even if internally "consistent" between the two eyes.

3. **It would still not tell us why culling/shadows are unstable** — that's a separate problem from eye-to-eye blur. The synced-pose toggle I just added addresses that directly (feed index 1 the real eyes' already-converged pose, read-only) without gambling on using index 1 as the *source of truth*.

## My recommendation

Test the toggle I just added first (`DiagApplySyncedPoseToExcludedViewIndex`) — it's the safer direction (real eyes are always the source of truth, index 1 just gets kept in sync with them, one-way). If that doesn't fix culling/shadows, then the "index 1 as authoritative source" experiment becomes worth trying, and I can add it as a separate toggle so you can A/B them independently. Want me to go ahead and add that second experimental mode now, or wait for results from the current one first?

## Why fast rotation specifically produces subtle blur

Look at the blend-alpha selection logic in `calculate_stereo_view_offset`:
```
blend_alpha = (is_hard_cut || force_full) ? 1.0 : get_native_stereo_fix_sync_pose_blend_alpha()
```

Your slider (`NativeStereoFixSyncPoseBlendAlpha`) defaults to **1.0**. That means **every single frame**, regardless of whether it's a "hard cut" or just normal continuous motion, Pass2 (right eye) is forced to **fully snap** to Pass1 (left eye)'s cached rotation/position — not blended, a hard 100% override.

Here's the subtlety: Pass1 and Pass2 are captured at two slightly different **times** within the same engine frame (Pass1 first, Pass2 second, back-to-back). During a thumbstick turn or a dash, the camera's rotation is changing continuously and fast. So:

- Pass1 captures the camera pose at time T.
- Pass2 (an instant later) forces its own pose to **exactly** Pass1's pose from time T — throwing away Pass2's own (slightly more current, slightly more rotated) live pose.
- Next frame, this repeats: left eye always renders the "true" live pose, right eye always renders a pose that's one small time-slice behind.

At rest, that lag is ~0 (nothing moved between Pass1 and Pass2), so it's invisible. But during **fast continuous rotation**, that per-frame lag becomes a small but non-zero constant angular offset between what the left eye sees and what the right eye sees — every frame, proportional to how fast you're turning. That's exactly "subtle blur, worse during dashing/fast thumbstick rotation" — it's not a hard desync (no double-vision snap), it's a persistent tiny right-eye lag that your visual system fuses into perceived blur rather than distinct diplopia.

This is a **different failure mode** than the hard-cut/zoom-snap issue — that one only fires on big sudden discontinuities (cutscenes, teleports); this one is present on **every frame** any time you're actively rotating/moving quickly, because `blend_alpha=1.0` applies unconditionally, not just during detected hard cuts.

## Why is index 1 polymorphic — what does it actually represent?

Based on everything the logs have shown, index 1 isn't a single engine concept at all — it's a **leftover numeric slot**, not a fixed semantic role like "left eye" or "shadow cascade #2." Here's the reasoning:

UE's `IStereoRendering::CalculateStereoViewOffset` is meant to be called once per eye for the primary game view family. But in this game's build, the hook is clearly being hit by **every consumer that queries the active stereo-rendering device for a view offset**, not just the two real eyes. That includes:

- The main stereo eyes (indices 2/3) — consistent, always full-res, always tied to `player_index=973137274`, always the same real `view_family`.
- Whatever secondary "next available slot" the engine hands out that frame to **any other view construction that happens to run while stereo is globally active** — UI icon/portrait render-to-texture widgets, shadow-view/light transform queries, etc.

The engine doesn't appear to assign these secondary callers a stable index — it just increments some internal call-counter within the frame and whichever caller shows up "next" gets numbered 1. That's why the *same* raw number (1) corresponded to a UI-icon-grid capture at one point in the log and a 990-calls-per-frame no-`FSceneView` caller at another point — they're unrelated systems that both happen to land in the same **numeric leftover bucket**, at different points in the session depending on what the game is doing (icons refreshing vs. shadows updating).

There isn't one "intended purpose" for index 1 — its intended purpose is whatever the calling subsystem's is; the number itself carries no persistent meaning. That's also why blocking it from **rendering** (early-return) caused no visible harm — none of its possible identities are a real eye.

## Why does NSF break on this while AFR doesn't?

This comes down to a structural difference in how each mode's pose-cache works:

**AFR (Alternate Frame Rendering):** renders exactly **one** eye per full engine frame, alternating left/right across *separate* frames. Its pose cache (`m_last_afr_rotation`) is a slow, frame-to-frame handoff — write this frame, read it back several frames later on the next same-parity frame. Even if a polymorphic index-1 caller also fires during an AFR frame, there's no tight timing collision: AFR's cache isn't expecting an immediate, same-frame partner write, so an extra unrelated write just gets overwritten again long before it's ever read back as the "real" cached eye pose.

**NSF (your two-pass native stereo fix):** renders **both** eyes within the *same single engine frame*, back-to-back, and the cache mechanism is deliberately a tight **same-frame handoff**: Pass1 (left) writes the cache, and microseconds later Pass2 (right) reads it. This narrow window is the entire point of the fix — it only works because nothing else is supposed to touch that cache slot in between. But since index 1 aliases onto the exact same cache slot (`true_index=0`) as the real left eye, if it fires **in between** Pass1 and Pass2 (which it clearly can, given it fires up to 990+ times in a single frame), it silently overwrites the left eye's just-cached pose with its own unrelated one — right before Pass2 reads it. That's the literal mechanism of the blur: the right eye ends up snapping to a stray icon/shadow transform's pose instead of the real left eye's pose, for that one frame.

AFR's slower, decoupled cache timing structurally can't be hit by this race; NSF's fast same-frame handoff design is exactly the kind of window this polymorphic extra caller can slip into.

That's exactly what proved index 1 "does NOT correspond to a visible rendered eye" — no stuck/frozen/blank eye resulted. **But it didn't fix the blur, and here's why:** the blur isn't caused by index 1 rendering something wrong — it's caused by index 1's call **racing with the real left eye's write to the shared pose cache** in between Pass1 and Pass2. But it does **not** stop whatever engine-side subsystem called index 1 in the first place from continuing to run its own logic that frame (icon capture / shadow view / whatever it is) — because early-returning our hook doesn't cancel the engine's outer call, it just makes *our* computed offset a no-op for that call. If that unrelated caller (icon capture, shadow view, etc.) actually *depends* on getting a valid transformed pose back to build its own render logic correctly, suppressing it entirely could leave that caller working with a wrong/stale pose too — but critically, **that doesn't affect the real eyes either way**, because full suppression *also* skips writing to the cache (same net effect on Pass1/Pass2 as the narrower fix). 

Given both approaches skip the cache-write, they should produce **the same fix for blur** — and that's consistent with what you found: neither full suppression nor cache-only-exclusion changes rendering of the real eyes, and either one should resolve the race. The real difference is scope of risk: full suppression also blocks whatever legitimate (if unrelated) work that caller needed from `calculate_stereo_view_offset`, which is unnecessary risk for zero additional benefit — hence why the narrower, cache-only exclusion is the better one to keep, not because full suppression doesn't work, but because it's an unnecessarily broader hammer for the same fix.

This is why calling the "original" wouldn't reveal anything new about index 1's identity — the original implementation has zero awareness of what index 1 represents; it would just apply arbitrary IPD math to whatever pose it's given, exactly as useless for a UI-icon-capture or shadow-view as our own replacement is.

## Is there a way to make index 1 "function correctly" in the stereo pathway?

Given what the evidence shows, **no — because index 1 isn't a stereo view to begin with**, so there's no "correct" stereo behavior to restore for it. You can't make a UI-icon-capture pipeline (stereo_pass=0/eSSP_FULL, is_real_stereo_family=false) or a shadow-cascade transform query into a "single-pass stereo option" — those systems were never rendering a user-facing eye; they're calling this function purely to get a pose transform for their own unrelated purpose. There's nothing to "fix" for index 1 as a renderable view because it was never meant to be one.

## Is there a legitimate alternate pathway to interact with it?

Yes, conceptually — if index 1 really is a shadow-cascade/light-view system (one of its two observed identities), the correct place to influence it isn't `CalculateStereoViewOffset` at all — it would be UE's actual shadow-setup code (`FProjectedShadowInfo`, `FSceneRenderer::InitViews`, or similar), which is a completely separate subsystem from stereo rendering. That's a much deeper, riskier hook to attempt (no existing infrastructure in this codebase touches it), and given tree-culling was unaffected either way when we tried influencing index 1's pose, there's no concrete evidence yet that doing so would fix anything - it would be exploratory, not a known fix.

## Bottom line

Index 1 is not an engine-intended "single-pass stereo view" waiting to be unlocked — it's incidental traffic from unrelated systems reusing the same hook entry point. The correct and complete fix for your reported symptom (blur/desync) is exactly what you already have: keep it from writing into the real eyes' shared pose cache (`DiagExcludeViewIndexFromSyncCache`), and leave everything else about it alone, since nothing else it's doing is stereo-rendering related.

# Wuthering Waves Native Stereo Fix — Double-Vision/Blur Investigation: Full History & Findings

## Background / Symptom

With Native Stereo Fix (NSF) enabled — the mod's non-AFR approach that renders both eyes as full independent scene passes rather than alternating frames — users reported a subtle but noticeable **double-vision/blur** effect. It was most apparent during:
- Dashing or fast camera-rotation motion via thumbstick
- Skill/ability VFX-heavy animations
- Cutscene/cinematic camera transitions
- Opening a UI menu shortly after a skill

It read as the right eye subtly "lagging" or being one frame/pose behind the left eye — a transient left/right eye pose mismatch rather than a constant, static offset.

---

## Attempt Log: What Was Tried, What Was Found, Why It Didn't Fully Work

### 1. Mirror-source bug (early, unrelated fix)
A bug in `D3D12Component.cpp` where the mirror fallback was pulling from the wrong source texture was found and fixed. This was a real bug but was **not** the cause of the reported double-vision — the symptom persisted after the fix.

### 2. Same-stereo-pass PRIMARY/PRIMARY (`m_native_stereo_fix_same_pass`)
Legacy approach: hide the view family from the `FSceneView` constructor and force `StereoPass=PRIMARY` on the secondary (right) eye's init options, so the engine treats both eyes identically.
- **Result:** Caused a full black-screen on both eyes (confirmed via `[VR][SAME-PASS-FORCE]` logging around `set_stereo_pass()`).
- **Verdict:** Rejected/unstable. Superseded by the Right Eye Shadow Fix approach. Kept in the UI only as a legacy/diagnostic option, off by default.

### 3. Extra-view index filtering (`DIAG: Suppress Extra View Index`)
Log evidence (`NSF-FINAL-EYE-POSE` + glitch-eye diagnostics) proved `calculate_stereo_view_offset()` is actually called **at least three times per frame** during NSF, not the expected two (one per eye). The hypothesis was that this extra call was a spurious render that could simply be suppressed/skipped.
- **Result:** The raw `view_index` assigned to this "extra" call was **not stable across sessions** — it was `3` in one capture, but in later sessions, blindly suppressing index `2` or `3` instead caused a **real eye to stick to the HMD** (confirmed in-headset).
- **Verdict:** Rejected as a general-purpose fix — too dangerous to hardcode a suppressed index without re-verifying every session. Kept as an off-by-default diagnostic toggle with a strong warning tooltip.

### 4. Projection-matrix divergence
Added logging to compare raw and final projection matrices for both eyes across many frames.
- **Result:** Projection matrices remained stable and consistent across the capture windows tested.
- **Verdict:** Ruled out — projection was not the cause.

### 5. World-to-meters (`world_to_meters`) mismatch (`DIAG: Log World-To-Meters Per-Eye`)
Hypothesis: if the two eyes' render calls saw different `world_to_meters` scale values within the same frame, that could produce a scale/offset mismatch that reads as blur/doubling.
- **Result:** Large-sample logging (`NSF-WTM-VALUE`, `NSF-WTM-MISMATCH`) showed no mismatch between eyes.
- **Verdict:** Ruled out.

### 6. Post-process / rendering feature tests (TAA, motion blur, DLSS, anti-aliasing)
Disabled each of these individually to A/B test whether they were amplifying or causing the doubled-image appearance.
- **Result:** No effect — issue persisted with all combinations disabled.
- **Verdict:** Ruled out as the root cause (though **Disable Motion Blur (Native Stereo Fix)** was kept as a permanent, sensible fix regardless — see "Toggles That Remain" below, since NSF never had AFR's automatic motion-blur-disable protection and a mono velocity buffer genuinely can cause independent per-eye blur trail divergence).

### 7. 2D screen mode test
Reproduced the symptom in 2D/desktop mode (not full stereo).
- **Result:** Blur/double-image behavior was still present.
- **Verdict:** Proved the issue was **not stereo-rendering-exclusive** — it pointed toward something in the camera-pose/animation update path rather than the stereo compositing itself.

### 8. Leftover scene-capture actor theory
Investigated whether a second, leftover scene-capture actor (from `UObjectHook.cpp`'s `spawn_actor` call sites) was rooted and firing redundant renders.
- **Result:** Confirmed there is only **one** real scene-capture actor spawn path; the other `spawn_actor` call sites are for adjustment visualizers/overlappers, unrelated to scene capture.
- **Verdict:** Ruled out.

### 9. Gradual hard-cut convergence (`DIAG: Gradual Hard-Cut Convergence`)
Once the sync-pose fix (see below) was working via an instant full snap on detected hard-cuts, tested whether ramping the correction in **linearly over ~1 second** (rather than snapping instantly) felt smoother.
- **Result:** Any **non-zero blend alpha** (i.e., anything less than a full, instant 1.0 snap) reintroduced the visible eye separation/blur during motion.
- **Verdict:** Rejected as the shipped default — the fix is sensitive to blend alpha, and only `alpha=1.0` (full snap) reliably eliminates the symptom. Kept as an off-by-default diagnostic toggle for further A/B testing.

### 10. `DiagApplySyncedPoseToExcludedViewIndex`
Once index 1 was excluded from the sync-pose cache (see below), tested feeding that excluded index the *same* fully-converged pose the real eyes settle on (read-only, without writing back into the cache) — theorizing this might fix secondary symptoms like inconsistent foliage/shadow-cascade culling attributed to that index.
- **Result:** No noticeable change to the blur when toggled.
- **Verdict:** Not the source of the fix; kept as an off-by-default diagnostic for future foliage/shadow-culling investigation, separate from the main blur fix.

---

## Deep-Dive: What Is `view_index=1`?

This became the central investigation once evidence showed NSF calls `calculate_stereo_view_offset()` more than twice per frame.

### Key diagnostics used
- **`NSF-RAW-VIEW-INDEX`** — unconditionally logs every raw `view_index` (0–8) the hook is called with, alongside `true_index`, `is_full_pass`, `is_using_afr`, and per-index call counts.
- **`NSF-TRUE-INDEX-ALIAS`** — logs when two different `view_index` values collide onto the same `true_index`.
- **`NSF-VIEWINDEX-IDENTITY`** — logs whether a given `view_index` is backed by a real `FSceneView`/`stereo_pass`, or looks like a sub-view/auxiliary pass.
- **`NSF-CALLER-SITE`** — logs the return-address (RVA) of the code that called into the hook, to see if different `view_index` values come from different call sites.
- **`NSF-STACKWALK-INDEX1`** — full stack-walk (via `RtlCaptureStackBackTrace`) specifically when `view_index=1` fires, bucketed by low-count vs. high-count per-frame call rates.

### Findings

1. **`true_index` is derived from `view_index`'s parity, not its raw value.** This means two *different* raw `view_index` values (e.g., `1` and `3`) can silently alias onto the same logical eye slot (`true_index`). `NSF-TRUE-INDEX-ALIAS` confirmed `view_index=1` racing with the real `view_index=3` eye call on the same `true_index` within the same frame — i.e., index 1's render call was **overwriting/competing with a real eye's cached pose** for that frame instead of being an ignorable third view.

2. **`view_index=1` is not a stable, single-purpose "eye."** Across different logging sessions it manifested differently:
   - In one session (`TextFile1.txt`), `NSF-VIEWINDEX-IDENTITY` showed `view_index=1` as a **64x64 tiled capture**, `stereo_pass=0`, `is_real_stereo_family=false` — consistent with a tiny non-stereo UI/utility-style capture, not a renderable eye.
   - In that same session, indices `2` and `3` were full-size, real stereo-family views (the actual left/right eyes).
   - In another session, `view_index=1` fired as a **very high-frequency burst** (900+ calls in a single frame at times), while in a later session (`TextFile3.txt`) it only fired 2–5 times per frame.
   - `NSF-CALLER-SITE` logging showed indices `1`, `2`, and `3` all originate from the **same executable return address** (`0x24868402`), meaning the engine calls the exact same code path for all of them — the *behavior* differs by index/context, not by a different call site.

3. **`view_index=1` never gets its own dedicated `FSceneView`.** Combined with its variable per-frame call count and non-eye tiled-capture appearance, this strongly suggests it corresponds to a **sub-view/auxiliary render pass** — plausibly something like a shadow-cascade pass, an occlusion/culling sub-view, or another per-frame utility view the engine's stereo rendering interception is incidentally intercepting alongside the two real eyes — **rather than a discrete, renderable third eye.**

4. **Excluding it from rendering entirely caused no visible regression.** Direct in-headset testing (a full early-return/skip on `view_index=1`) produced **no stuck, frozen, or blank eye**. This is important corroborating evidence that index 1 is not load-bearing for either eye's actual visual output.

5. **Its exact underlying engine subsystem was not conclusively pinned down.** The stack-walk diagnostic (`NSF-STACKWALK-INDEX1`) works, but a single session's capture (`TextFile3.txt`) only reproduced a low-count sample (2 calls/frame) rather than the earlier high-frequency burst (900+/frame) seen in `TextFile1.txt`. This means index 1's calling pattern is itself context-dependent (varies by what's happening in the scene — likely tied to whatever triggers the auxiliary pass, e.g., shadow-casting geometry present/absent), and further multi-session stack-walk data would be needed to name the exact subsystem definitively. This remains an open question for future investigation, but it does **not** block the blur fix, which does not depend on knowing index 1's exact purpose — only on excluding it from the pose-sync race.

### What this suggests
`view_index=1`'s render call was intermittently **hijacking the sync-pose cache** meant for the two real eyes (because its `true_index` parity aliases onto a real eye's slot), overwriting a real eye's cached pose with a sub-view's pose mid-frame. This produced the momentary left/right desync — read as blur/double-vision — especially during motion, when the sub-view's pose could differ meaningfully from the real eye's pose in that instant.

---

## The Implemented Fix

Two complementary mechanisms, combined:

### 1. Sync Eye Pose During Camera Transitions (`NativeStereoFixSyncPose`)
Caches the left eye's (Pass 1) camera rotation **and** position for the current frame and forces the right eye (Pass 2) to reuse both, instead of independently re-sampling the live animated camera for its own render call.
- Both position and rotation **must** be synced together — direct in-headset testing with a manual Camera Freeze debug tool proved that freezing only one of the two still produced the desync, since a camera pose is the combination of both, and correcting only one still leaves the two eyes rendering from different world transforms.
- The position sync is applied **before** the per-eye IPD/eye-separation offset, so stereo depth/parallax is preserved — this only fixes the transient pose desync, not normal per-eye separation.
- Controlled by a blend alpha (`NativeStereoFixSyncPoseBlendAlpha`): `1.0` = Pass2 fully snaps to Pass1's pose (eliminates desync but can read as one-sided lag for that frame); lower values let Pass2 keep some live motion. **Testing showed only `1.0` reliably eliminates the visible blur** — the gradual-convergence experiment (see Attempt #9) proved any partial blend reintroduces separation.

### 2. Exclude View Index From Sync-Pose Cache (`DiagExcludeViewIndexFromSyncCache`, index = 1)
Excludes the specified `view_index` (defaulted/forced to `1`) from ever writing to or reading from the NSF sync-pose cache used by `calculate_stereo_view_offset()`. Critically, this does **not** skip rendering of that index (unlike the rejected Attempt #3) — it only removes it from the pose-cache race, which is what was actually causing the corruption. This is why it's safe: in-headset testing confirmed fully suppressing `view_index=1`'s *rendering* caused no stuck/frozen/blank eye, so excluding it from just the *cache* is strictly safer and non-disruptive.

### Why the combination works
- The Sync Pose fix ensures both real eyes agree on a single, consistent pose per frame (eliminating the primary source of desync from independent re-sampling).
- The cache-exclusion fix removes the confounding factor that was corrupting that shared cache in the first place — `view_index=1`'s aliasing render call — so the sync-pose cache can only ever be written/read by the two real eyes, never overwritten mid-frame by the auxiliary sub-view pass.

Both must be active together for the fix to be reliable, which is why they were bundled into a single master toggle (see below), rather than left as two toggles a user could enable independently and get inconsistent results.

---

## Toggles That Remain

### Native Stereo Fix section (main menu — kept minimal/production-facing)
| Toggle | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Enabled** | Master NSF on/off |

| **Disable Motion Blur (Native Stereo Fix)** | Prevents per-eye motion-blur-trail divergence (NSF lacked AFR's automatic protection here) |

## Open Questions for Future Work
- The exact engine subsystem `view_index=1` belongs to (shadow cascade pass? occlusion culling sub-view? something else?) is still not conclusively named — only its *behavior* (non-eye, variable call count, no dedicated `FSceneView`, safe to exclude/suppress) is established. More multi-session `NSF-STACKWALK-INDEX1` captures (ideally during both the low-count and high-count firing patterns) would be needed to pin this down.
- Whether `DiagApplySyncedPoseToExcludedViewIndex` has any real benefit for foliage-sway/shadow-cascade culling artifacts (separate from the blur fix) is unresolved — it showed no effect on blur but wasn't specifically tested against culling symptoms.

1. **A single frame took over 10.6 seconds to complete** (`FRAME PACING over 10655ms`). That's not a UEVR hitch — that's the underlying engine's render thread (or GPU work queue) genuinely stalling, almost certainly due to heavy level-streaming/shader-compilation work during the map transition (asset loading, PSO cache misses, texture streaming, etc. — all things UE4 does synchronously enough to block the render thread on a cold/uncached level load).

2. **Present() itself then failed** (`Present failed: -7785fffb`) immediately after that spike. This is the classic signature of the GPU driver's own watchdog (TDR) deciding the GPU has been "stuck" too long and resetting/removing the device — Windows' TDR default timeout is ~2 seconds of an unresponsive GPU queue, and a 10+ second frame absolutely can trigger that.

3. **The repeated "present stalled for 5000+ms" / "engine tick stalled" messages afterward** are the mod's own watchdog trying to recover — but the tick truly isn't resuming, because the device is already gone/hung underneath it. This is the aftermath, not the cause.

4. **Crash location**: `D3D12Resources.cpp:596`, "hr failed... DXGI_ERROR_DEVICE_REMOVED... Reason: DXGI_ERROR_DEVICE_HUNG" is UE4's own D3D12RHI code detecting that a resource operation (likely a `Map`/`Unmap`, resource creation, or a fence wait) got back the removed-device HRESULT and fatal-errors out. This is UE4 crashing on its own once the device is already gone — it's a *symptom*, not something the mod directly threw.

### Why this is plausible with UEVR in the mix specifically

Your codebase's own comments in `FFakeStereoRenderingHook.cpp` (around `create_scene_capture()`, lines ~12447-12507) describe **exactly this failure mode** as previously-observed and already partially mitigated:
- A tick-stall flicker during a level transition could let a scene-capture recreation (new SRV/RTV descriptor heaps, texture rebinding) slip through mid-stall.
- That recreation work landing on the same frame (or the frame right after) a multi-second GPU stall was directly observed to precede a `DXGI_ERROR_DEVICE_REMOVED`/`DEVICE_HUNG` crash in earlier testing — which is why the cooldown (3000ms), the 15-consecutive-non-stalled-check requirement, and the "refuse to recreate while stalled" guard all exist.
- There's also a note about avoiding recreating scene-capture resources while a view-target reallocation (resolution change) is still pending, because doing so with mismatched old/new resolutions was observed to fail SRV descriptor heap creation and take the whole device down.

That's consistent with the level transition being unusually heavy this time (map/scene complexity, shader compilation, asset streaming) — heavy enough that even with the existing guards, the underlying GPU work queue itself backed up for 10+ seconds, which is largely outside the mod's control once it happens (the guards prevent the mod from making it *worse* by doing more GPU work mid-stall, but they can't prevent the engine's own loading work from stalling the GPU in the first place).

- This is most likely a **genuine GPU-side stall (TDR) during a heavy level transition**, not a straightforward logic bug in the mod — your own code already has substantial guardrails against the mod's scene-capture recreation making this worse, and the log shows those guards did trigger (throttling, refusing to recreate while stalled).

- Common real-world contributors to this exact crash signature (worth checking, independent of any code change): GPU driver version/stability, VRAM pressure (headset + desktop mirror + high-res NSF scene capture doubling render target memory), thermal throttling, and background GPU load from other processes during heavy asset streaming.

The 15-consecutive-check gate (`required_consecutive_non_stalled_checks = 15`) at 750ms polling granularity means the code waits roughly **11+ seconds of apparent tick stability** before allowing scene-capture recreation again after a stall. Given your log shows a **10.6-second single-frame spike**, that's within the range this 15-check gate was specifically designed to survive — so on paper the mitigation should have applied. Each cycle re-runs the full `create_dummy_device()` → `CreateDXGIFactory` → `CreateCommandQueue` → dummy swapchain → vtable-offset discovery sequence in `D3D12Hook.cpp`. The first three attempts got torn down and retried because `Framework::hook_monitor()`'s "present stalled" watchdog (5-6 second thresholds) kept firing before the *real* game swapchain had actually been created yet — this is a bootstrap-timing race, not a bug exactly, but it means the mod is doing **3x the dummy-device/factory/queue/swapchain creation work** it needs to during a normal launch, adding ~25+ seconds of redundant work (mostly spent inside `D3D12CreateDevice`, which is the slow part — 5.5s on the first attempt, 1.8-2.4s on later ones).

**Why this happens:** the very first "present stalled" log at `16:12:32.731` reports `7721643ms` (over 2 hours) — that's an uninitialized/stale `m_last_present_time` default, so the watchdog's very first check is guaranteed to immediately declare a stall and force an unnecessary rehook attempt before the game has even had a chance to present a frame. This is purely a startup-sequencing artifact.

## 2. 130 repeated "Bad binding passed to xrSuggestInteractionProfileBindings" warnings

Every one of these is the OpenXR runtime rejecting an unsupported input-path binding (Go controller, Vive controller, KHR simple controller, etc.) for various actions. These are logged individually per-action, per-unsupported-profile, at `info` level during controller/action-set setup (~line 300-700+). Not something the mod can eliminate structurally (the profiles genuinely aren't supported by the connected runtime), but a large volume of these does add avoidable log I/O and spdlog formatting overhead during startup, and clutters diagnosis of the real timing.

## 3. "Failed to get type info: unknown exception" repeats on every rehook attempt

Logged once per D3D12 hook attempt (3 times in this log) right after querying the dummy swapchain. This is swallowed/non-fatal (execution continues normally afterward), but it means a C++ exception is actually being thrown and caught during a normal startup path each time — exception throw/catch is comparatively expensive, and doing it 3x during init is wasted cycles, though at this scale (milliseconds) it's not itself a meaningful contributor to the 30+ second startup.

## Summary — is this actionable?
- The dominant cost (~25s+) is `D3D12CreateDevice` being genuinely slow (driver/shader-cache JIT on cold start) combined with the watchdog's stale initial timestamp causing 2 unnecessary extra full rehook cycles before the real swapchain exists.
- If you want, the concrete, low-risk fix would be initializing `m_last_present_time`/`m_last_chance_time` to "now" (or skipping the very first stall check) at Framework construction instead of leaving it default-constructed to the epoch, so the watchdog doesn't fire an immediate false-positive stall before the game has even presented once. That alone would likely cut out at least the first of the three rehook cycles.
- The XR binding warnings and the swallowed exception are cosmetic/non-blocking and not worth touching unless you want cleaner logs.

Here's what `sync pose` actually does and why the residual blur happens, plus a concrete way to reduce it.

## What sync pose does today (asymmetric, not "averaged")

Looking at `calculate_stereo_view_offset()` (line ~9386 onward):

- **Pass1 (left eye, `true_index==0`)** always renders first with its own live camera rotation. Its pose is just cached (`m_nsf_sync_pose_rotation_double`, etc.) — never modified.
- **Pass2 (right eye, `true_index==1`)** runs immediately after, and is forced to match Pass1's *cached* pose via `blend_alpha`. When a hard cut is detected (or `force_full`), `blend_alpha=1.0`, meaning Pass2's rotation is **completely overwritten** with Pass1's rotation (line 9518-9519: `*rot_d = hook_data.m_nsf_sync_pose_rotation_double;`).

So the left eye is *always* the "reference"/dominant eye, and the right eye is always the one snapped into agreement. That's exactly the "one eye dominant" issue you're describing — it's not symmetric syncing, it's unilateral correction.

## Why true "average both eyes" isn't directly possible

Pass1 has already been submitted to the GPU by the time Pass2's data exists — you can't retroactively change what Pass1 rendered. So a literal "compute the average of both eyes' poses and apply it to both" isn't achievable within a single render call sequence.

## What IS achievable and should reduce the dash/fast-turn blur

Two real, implementable options that reduce the "one-eye-yanked-into-place" artifact without reintroducing the double-vision (recall: any blend_alpha < 1.0 was already shown to reintroduce visible separation):

1. **Extrapolate the sync target instead of using the stale captured pose.** Right now Pass2 snaps to whatever Pass1's rotation was *at Pass1's render time*, which is already slightly "behind" by the time Pass2 fires (that's the residual gap during fast rotation — the camera kept moving between Pass1 and Pass2). We track a rotation-delta EMA already (`m_nsf_pose_delta_rot_ema`); we could use that plus elapsed time between Pass1/Pass2 to extrapolate Pass1's pose forward to "now," so Pass2 snaps to a *predicted current* pose instead of a *stale past* pose. This keeps the full 1.0-strength snap (still zero L/R divergence, still fixes double vision) but the snap target itself is closer to where the camera actually is, so it should look less like a jarring blur/judder during dash/fast-turn frames.

2. **Alternate which eye is the reference every hard-cut event** (instead of always forcing left→right), so the "snap" is distributed across both eyes over time rather than the right eye always being the one visibly corrected. This won't reduce the blur itself, but addresses your "one eye not dominant" framing directly.

Option 1 is the one most likely to actually reduce the perceived blur during dashes, since it targets the root cause (stale reference pose) rather than just which eye gets corrected.

Want me to implement option 1 (velocity-extrapolated sync target) as a new toggle-gated diagnostic, consistent with how the other NSF experiments were added?

## What I implemented

**New toggle: "Velocity-Extrapolated Sync Pose"** (Debug tab → NS Double Vision Diagnostics), off by default, plus a slider for max extrapolation window (default 33ms ≈ 1 frame @ 30fps).

**How it works:**
1. Every time Pass1 (left eye) caches its pose, `update_nsf_sync_pose_velocity()` now also computes the camera's angular velocity (deg/sec for yaw/pitch/roll) by comparing this Pass1 pose to the *previous* Pass1 pose, using the real wall-clock time elapsed between them. A sanity guard rejects the estimate if the time delta is near-zero or absurdly large (e.g. after a loading hitch).
2. When Pass2 (right eye) goes to snap to Pass1's cached pose, instead of always using the exact pose Pass1 had at its call time (which is already stale by a few ms once fast dash/turn motion is happening), it can now call `get_nsf_extrapolated_sync_rotation()`, which extrapolates that cached pose forward by however much time has passed since it was cached — clamped to the max-extrapolation slider so a hitching frame can't extrapolate wildly.
3. This is applied identically in both the double-precision and single-precision code paths, and it still performs a full-strength (or blended) snap — it doesn't reintroduce any L/R divergence, it just corrects *what* Pass2 snaps to.

This is purely additive and toggle-gated (mirrors how the other NSF experiments were introduced), so it can be A/B tested in-headset during dash/fast-turn without touching the existing default behavior. ## New toggle: "Post-Hard-Cut Sensitivity Boost" (Debug tab → NS Double Vision Diagnostics)

- **Off by default.**
- When enabled: after a hard-cut divergence event fires (the same trigger that already drives auto-mirror-on-motion), the spike-detector's sensitivity multiplier is temporarily lowered (default 2.0x instead of the normal 6.0x baseline) for a configurable window (default 500ms).
- During that window, smaller residual Pass1/Pass2 divergence — the kind that normally falls back to the gentler blend_alpha slider — now also gets treated as a hard cut and receives the full-strength snap.
- Outside the window, behavior is completely unchanged (back to the normal 6.0x threshold).
- Two tunable sliders: **Sensitivity Boost Window (ms)** and **Sensitivity Boost Multiplier (x0.1)**, so you can tune exactly how long/how sensitive the boosted period is.

## New capture tool: NumPad1 (arm) + NumPad2 (mark)

**How to use it in-headset:**
1. Press **NumPad1** the instant you begin a dash (or right before). This arms an unthrottled per-frame capture of every relevant sync-pose value for the next 200 frames (~3 seconds at 60-90fps) or 3 seconds, whichever hits first.
2. Press **NumPad2** the instant you actually perceive the visual blur. This doesn't stop the capture — it just tags that exact frame's log line with `[MARK]` so we can find precisely where in the sequence the blur happened.
3. After the dash, grab the log and search for `[VR][DASH-CAPTURE]` — you'll get one line per frame with:
   - `rot_delta_deg` / `pos_delta` — the raw Pass1↔Pass2 divergence that frame
   - `rot_ema` / `pos_ema` — the rolling baseline the spike detector compares against
   - `is_hard_cut` — whether the spike detector fired that frame
   - `blend_alpha` — the actual blend strength applied
   - `pass1_rot` vs `pass2_rot_before` — the two raw rotations being reconciled, so we can see the real magnitude of what's being snapped

The `[MARK]` line lets us see exactly what `rot_delta`/`is_hard_cut`/`blend_alpha` looked like at the moment you perceived blur, and the surrounding ~10-20 frames of context show us the lead-up and aftermath (e.g., is it a sustained high blend_alpha, a single violent snap, oscillating hard_cut true/false, etc.).
