## What the capture shows

Looking at the two ARMED capture windows around lines 14293 and 14571 (during your dash+spin repro):
```
frame=14276 rot_delta_deg=0.0000 pos_delta=15.07  is_hard_cut=false blend_alpha=1.000
frame=14278 rot_delta_deg=0.0000 pos_delta=14.24  is_hard_cut=false blend_alpha=1.000
frame=14280 rot_delta_deg=0.0000 pos_delta=14.92  is_hard_cut=false blend_alpha=1.000
...
frame=14522 rot_delta_deg=0.0000 pos_delta=27.34  is_hard_cut=false blend_alpha=1.000
frame=14524 rot_delta_deg=0.0000 pos_delta=31.17  is_hard_cut=false blend_alpha=1.000
```

Two important patterns, consistent across **every single frame** in both windows:

1. **`rot_delta_deg` is always 0.0000.** The blur isn't rotational — dashing doesn't create a rotation mismatch between the two stereo passes.
2. **`pos_delta` is consistently large (14–31 units) on *every* frame**, not just a one-off spike. `is_hard_cut` never fires because the EMA baseline (`pos_ema` ~16-19) has already adapted to treat this level of delta as "normal," so the hard-cut gate never trips — yet `blend_alpha` stays pinned at 1.000 the whole time.

## Why this causes blur specifically during dashes

`pos_delta` is the position difference between pass1 (left eye, cached) and pass2 (right eye) for the *same frame*. During normal camera movement this is small because both eyes are sampled close together in time. During a dash, the character/camera is moving fast enough that by the time pass2 is computed, the "true" position has already advanced 15-30 units past where pass1 was cached.

With sync pose's full snap (`blend_alpha=1.0`), pass2 is forcibly overwritten with pass1's *stale* position every frame. That's fine for a one-frame hard cut (teleport/scene change), but during sustained fast motion it means the corrected eye is continuously forced ~15-30 units *behind* where it should actually be, frame after frame — a persistent, velocity-proportional lag between eyes, which reads visually as smear/blur. It's not a discontinuity glitch; it's a continuous parallax-timing offset that the snap corrector is misidentifying as noise and is stomping on every frame.

This matches exactly what you observed: turning sync pose off removes the blur during dashes (because the natural small pass1/pass2 timing offset isn't being forcibly overwritten), while it's still needed for the original hard-cut double-vision case.

## Recommended fix

Don't touch `view_index=1` — this is purely a sync-pose gating problem. The fix should distinguish **sustained high-velocity motion** (dash) from an actual **one-frame discontinuity** (hard cut/teleport), and only apply the full snap for the latter:

- Add a "sustained motion" detector: if `pos_delta` stays elevated above baseline for N consecutive frames (rather than being an isolated one-frame spike), treat it as legitimate dash motion and skip/reduce the snap (e.g., don't override pass2's position, or blend at a much lower alpha) rather than forcing `blend_alpha=1.0`.
- Keep the current instant hard-cut/snap behavior only for genuine single-frame teleport-style jumps (large delta appearing suddenly after a stable low-delta history).

Want me to implement this "sustained-motion vs single-frame-cut" distinction in `FFakeStereoRenderingHook.cpp`/`.hpp` (using the existing EMA/hard-cut infrastructure), so sync pose keeps fixing the original double-vision case but stops snapping during dashes?

## Two independent, A/B-testable fixes for dash blur

Both toggles are in **Debug → NS Double Vision Diagnostics**, off by default, and can be enabled one at a time (or together) to compare against each other and against the current behavior.

**Fix #1 — "Rotation-Gated Position Sync"**
Every frame, if `rot_delta_deg` is below the threshold slider (default 1.0°), the position snap is skipped entirely for that frame (rotation sync is untouched). Since real hard cuts always show a rotation spike in the capture data, and dashes never do, this should cleanly separate the two cases on a per-frame basis.

**Fix #2 — "Sustained-Motion Position Sync Suppression"**
Tracks a running streak of consecutive low-rotation frames (same threshold). Once the streak hits the configured count (default 3 frames), position sync gets suppressed for the rest of the streak. A single frame with real rotation divergence immediately resets the streak, so genuine hard cuts still snap instantly — this just adds a tiny grace period before suppression kicks in, which may feel smoother if a real cut has one noisy near-zero-rotation frame at its very start.

## How to test

1. Enable only **Fix #1**, try dashing/spinning, and re-trigger the NumPad2 marker on a genuine glitch (e.g. a skill/camera-transition) to confirm it still gets fixed.
2. Turn off Fix #1, enable only **Fix #2**, repeat.
3. Compare which feels smoother during dashes while still fixing the original double-vision case.
4. You can also tune the threshold slider if 1.0° turns out to be too strict/loose, and the sustained-motion frame count if fix #2 needs more/less delay.

## Summary of what was fixed

Your log revealed the exact gap: one of your NumPad2 marks (frame 18186-18238) was a **purely positional hard cut** — `pos_delta` spiked to 300-455 units while `rot_delta_deg` stayed under 0.12°. The remaining faint blur here isn't a suppression-logic failure — it's the small residual cost of the full snap itself: on an extremely fast translation like this, Pass1's cached position is already one frame stale by the time Pass2 renders, so even a perfect snap leaves a tiny one-frame-old positional error proportional to velocity. The faster the underlying motion, the bigger that unavoidable one-frame lag becomes. This is a fundamentally different, much smaller issue than the previous full double-vision — it's the "eye momentarily lags a hair behind an extremely fast dash" cost you'd expect from any single-cached-frame correction, not a gating bug.

3. Leave the ceiling alone — raising it would just reopen the double-vision gap on this same case, since 371-563 needs to stay above whatever ceiling you pick.

- **Why dash/turns look blurry**: continuous motion causes the same small divergence every frame (not a one-off cut), so naive snapping fights normal parallax constantly.

**1. The trigger** — right as you opened the menu, the game's own code (`Client-Win64-Shipping.exe`, not UEVR) hit two access violations back-to-back at RVA `0x23e1f90e` and `0x23e1f91a` (10 bytes apart, almost certainly the same statement: a load then a store against the same stale object). This is the "Exception Handler" in `FFakeStereoRenderingHook.cpp` (~line 8025) — a vectored exception handler that catches known use-after-free (UAF) crashes in the game exe and tries to keep it running by forcing the faulting load to return `0` or skipping the faulting store entirely, rather than letting the OS terminate the process.

**2. Why it still died** — the recovery patched over *two* individual instructions, but it has no way to know whether the object those instructions were operating on (whatever menu/widget got freed) is needed correctly a few instructions/frames later elsewhere in the game's own logic. In this case the game didn't crash immediately, but its state was now corrupted enough that **rendering hung** — from `21:06:39` onward, `Framework::hook_monitor()` reports `present stalled for ~5000ms` on a 5-second loop forever, meaning the swapchain never presented another frame again. **3. Why no crash dump exists** — because the process never actually hard-crashed (SEH-terminated); the vectored handler swallowed the access violation and returned `EXCEPTION_CONTINUE_EXECUTION`, so Windows/the game's own crash reporter never saw a fatal exception. - This is **RVA `0x23e1f90e`/`0x23e1f91a`** in the game's exe — a new address not previously seen (the comment in the handler notes it already recovers `0x23e1f889`, `0x23e2aa86`, etc., so this is another instance of the same recurring UAF family, likely tied to some UI/menu object being freed while still referenced).

Short answer: **conceptually yes, and it's actually a good diagnosis** — but it's a bigger architectural change than what's currently patched in, and there's already evidence in this codebase that the "properly integrated" version of this idea was tried and crashed.

Here's why it's relevant:

**Why both symptoms have the same root cause**

Right now NSF renders each eye as a **separate, decoupled `BeginRenderViewFamily` call** (Pass1 = left, Pass2 = right), each its own `FSceneViewFamily`/scene capture, not two views inside one shared family the way real stereo rendering (and everything UE's stereo/`ISceneViewExtension` machinery assumes) works. That single architectural fact explains both bugs you're chasing:

- **Shadow lighting missing an eye**: whole-scene shadow setup only runs once per view family, gated on "am I the shadow-owning (primary) view." Since Pass2 is its own family with the view marked SECONDARY, it never gets that setup — hence the `Right Eye Shadow Fix` you already have, which manually flips the view's cached primary/secondary/StereoPass fields (`sceneview_xref::eye_fields`) after the fact so the engine *thinks* it's primary. That's a workaround for the family being split, not a fix of the split itself.
- **Blur/pose divergence**: because Pass1 and Pass2 are two separate render calls issued at different points in the same engine tick, the camera/animation state can have moved between them (that's exactly what `NSF-POSE-DIVERGE` is measuring). If both eyes were views inside **one** `SetupView`/`BeginRenderViewFamily` call (as `ISceneViewExtension::SetupViewFamily`/`SetupView` is designed for), they'd necessarily share the same frame snapshot — no divergence possible, no sync-pose cache/blend-alpha hacks needed at all.

**Why it isn't already done that way**

The comments in `FFakeStereoRenderingHook.cpp` show this was tried: `m_native_stereo_fix_same_pass` ("Use Same Stereo Pass (unstable)") hid the view family from the `FSceneView` constructor and forced `PRIMARY` on the secondary view's init options — and it null-derefs inside the engine. That's the "do it properly via one shared view family" attempt, and it crashed, which is presumably why Right Eye Shadow Fix + sync-pose exist as the fallback/patch approach instead.

**Is a real `ISceneViewExtension` a viable path forward?**

Possibly, but it's a different mechanism than the `same_pass` attempt: instead of forcing the *existing* Pass2 view into PRIMARY, you'd register a genuine extension object (the codebase already has the vtable-hijack scaffolding for this in `SceneViewExtensionAnalyzer`/`g_view_extension_vtable`) and implement `IsActiveThisFrame`/`SetupViewFamily`/`BeginRenderViewFamily_RenderThread` to run the shadow-owning setup logic for Pass2 directly, rather than flipping cached fields after construction. That's lower-risk than forcing PRIMARY on the actual struct (which is what crashed), because it works through the engine's intended extension hook rather than mutating internal state it doesn't expect touched.

If you want, I can look at what `sceneview_xref::eye_fields` actually contains and whether the shadow-owning logic is something callable directly from an extension hook (rather than field-flip), which would be the safer half-step toward this idea. Want me to dig into that?

Good — I found the actual mechanics. Here's what `sceneview_xref::eye_fields` really is and why it changes the calculus a bit:

**What `eye_fields` actually is**

It's not a semantic list of "shadow ownership fields" — it's built purely empirically: `resolve_live()` diffs every 4-byte dword between the live Pass1 (`v0`) and Pass2 (`v1`) `FSceneView` structs and records every offset where the values differ (`eye_fields.push_back({i, a, b})` at line 6514, called from wherever the full diff runs). So `eye_fields` = "every field that happens to differ between the two eye views this session," which then gets flipped indiscriminately (mask-gated) during Pass2 to make the engine believe it's still the left/primary eye. There's no dedicated "shadow owner" flag identified — it's `StereoPass` + whatever cached copies/flags happen to also differ, lumped together under one bitmask.

**Why this matters for your ISceneViewExtension idea**

This confirms the current fix is a **black-box struct patch**, not a real ISceneViewExtension implementation. A real `SetupViewFamily`/`BeginRenderViewFamily_RenderThread` override wouldn't need any of this offset-diffing — it would let you call the engine's actual shadow-setup logic through its intended entry point, working on real fields with known semantics instead of "whatever offset differed on this game build." That's a legitimate stability upgrade over field-flipping.

**However — here's the catch for implementing it now**

The `SceneViewExtensionAnalyzer` scaffolding you have hijacks the vtable of an **existing** extension already registered by the engine, and only proves generic slots (`IsActiveThisFrame`, `BeginRenderViewFamily`, `PreRenderViewFamily_RenderThread`) can be called — it doesn't give you a spot to inject "run primary-eye shadow setup for Pass2." The actual UE shadow-owner logic lives deep inside `FSceneRenderer`/`FDeferredShadingSceneRenderer::InitViews`, gated on `View.bIsSceneCapture`/`ViewFamily.Views[0]==this` style checks — not something an extension callback exposes a hook for. An extension can influence view setup (matrices, post-process, primitive visibility) but it can't force the engine's internal "first view in family" shadow cache logic to also run for a second, independently-submitted family, because Pass2 literally isn't in the same `ViewFamily.Views` array as Pass1.

**Bottom line**

The real fix for both bugs is unifying Pass1/Pass2 into one `FSceneViewFamily` with `Views[0]` and `Views[1]` (true stereo, not two decoupled captures) — which is exactly what `m_native_stereo_fix_same_pass` attempted and crashed on. `ISceneViewExtension` is a legitimate architectural direction, but it's a *replacement* for that same-pass merge, not an incremental patch you can bolt onto the current two-family design — it would need the same "put both eyes in one family" restructuring underneath it to actually give the extension a family where `Views[0]` is the real primary. Given the crash history on that exact code path, I'd treat this as a full re-architecture task (worth planning separately with a fallback/rollback strategy) rather than a quick toggle addition. Want me to scope that as a proper investigation/plan, or leave the current field-flip + sync-pose patches as the pragmatic solution for now?

**Why, per their own conclusion (verbatim reasoning in the code):**

> "The real problem is structural: with two views flagged PRIMARY in the same family, whatever per-family shadow/base-pass setup keys off `StereoPass==PRIMARY` can only fully render one of them, silently dropping or misdirecting the other eye's render — exactly matching the reported symptoms. There is no known safe way to make the engine treat two views as PRIMARY simultaneously without patching that internal (unsymboled) engine logic directly."

So this isn't a hook-ordering bug or a state leak they missed — it's that UE's `FSceneRenderer`/base-pass-setup internals structurally assume **exactly one** primary view per family, and that assumption is baked into unsymboled, closed-source engine code they'd have to reverse-engineer and patch directly (not just flip a flag) to support two-primary. **Conclusion**

Given this is already proven and documented as a genuine engine-internal constraint (not a workaround gap), a real fix would require disassembling and patching the specific internal function(s) that gate shadow/base-pass setup on `StereoPass==PRIMARY` — a much larger, riskier reverse-engineering effort than an ISceneViewExtension wrapper, and with no guarantee it's even safely patchable without breaking other rendering paths.

I read through `TextFile4.txt` and cross-referenced it against the actual code paths in `FFakeStereoRenderingHook.cpp`. Here's what's actually happening — no further logs needed, the two symptoms come from two different (but related) root causes:

## 1. Why the right-eye shadow fix is inconsistent

Look at [FFakeStereoRenderingHook.cpp](src/mods/vr/FFakeStereoRenderingHook.cpp) around line 7647-7675, the actual fix logic:
```cpp
for (size_t i = 0; i < fields.size(); ++i) {
    if (i < 32 && (mask & (1u << i)) == 0) continue;
    const auto& f = fields[i];
    auto p = (uint32_t*)((uintptr_t)pass2_view + f.offset);
    if (*p == f.right) {
        pass2_restore.emplace_back(p, *p);
        *p = f.left;
    }
}
```

This only flips a field if the live Pass2 view *currently* holds exactly the value `f.right` that was captured once by `sceneview_xref`. Your log confirms two things:
- `flipped 3/12 eye fields (mask=fb)` — of the 12 fields `sceneview_xref` empirically discovered (a brute-force dword diff, not a semantic map — see line 6488/6517), only 3 actually matched `f.right` this frame and got flipped. The other fields either already held `f.left` (nothing to do — harmless) or held some *third* value that isn't `f.left` or `f.right` (silently skipped — the flip doesn't happen for that field this frame).
- `eye fields not yet resolved by sceneview_xref` appears too — meaning on some runs/frames `sceneview_xref::eye_fields` is still empty when Pass2 fires, so the fix is a complete no-op until resolution completes (`feed()`/`resolve` is attempt-limited and timing-dependent, not guaranteed to finish before the first few Pass2 calls).

So the fix's behavior is entirely state-dependent on whatever transient values those 12 dwords happen to hold *this specific frame*. `eye_fields` was built from a **single snapshot diff** of Pass1 vs Pass2 (line 6440-6469: differences where both values are small ints < 8), and several of those fields are not stable per-eye identity — they're transient per-frame state (visibility flags, culling counters, LOD indices, etc. that just happened to differ that one time). That's why:
- Sometimes it "works" — the fields that matter for shadow ownership happen to be among the 3 that flip correctly that frame.
- Sometimes it "fails to fix NSF-on shadows" — the actual shadow-ownership field wasn't in the flipped set this frame (held a third value, or wasn't part of the original snapshot diff at all).
- Sometimes it "breaks NSF-off shadows" — when NSF is toggled off, `is_native_stereo_fix_right_eye_shadows_enabled()` should gate this off too (it's called unconditionally inside the `if` at line 7647), but if that toggle is somehow still true or evaluated with stale state, flipping fields that used to mean "eye identity" under NSF's frame layout now corrupts a differently-laid-out Pass2 view under the non-NSF path, since `eye_fields` was resolved under one rendering mode and reused for another.

**Root cause:** `eye_fields` is a one-time empirical guess, not a semantically verified per-frame ownership map, so its correctness is coincidental and mode-dependent.

## 2. Why "scene view extension compatibility" attaches the left eye to the HMD

This is `is_sceneview_compatibility_enabled()`, handled at line 6772-6842. Look at how `true_index` is computed (line 6762-6770):
```cpp
auto& last_index = g_hook->m_sceneview_data.last_index;
if (last_frame_count != g_frame_count || last_index > 1) {
    last_index = 0;
}
last_frame_count = g_frame_count;
const auto true_index = vr->is_using_afr() ? (g_frame_count + last_index) % 2 : last_index;
...
last_index++;  // (line 7024, end of function)
```

`true_index` — which decides *which HMD eye's pose/projection gets written into this FSceneView* — is derived purely from **call order** within the frame (0 for the first `sceneview_constructor` call, 1 for the second), not from any actual eye/stereo-pass identity read off the view itself. This assumes the engine always constructs exactly two views per frame in strict Left-then-Right order, with nothing else calling the constructor in between.

That assumption breaks whenever the engine constructs a scene view for something else in between the two stereo passes (shadow depth passes, reflection captures, scene-capture-actor views — all of which also go through this same constructor, as your logs elsewhere show `LGUI_REDIRECT_STATS`/`LGUI_A3_LIFECYCLE` reuse indicating heavy scene/actor churn). If any such extra view construction happens before the "real" second (right) view, `last_index` increments past what you intend, and the real right-eye view ends up getting `true_index == 0` (left eye's HMD pose) written into it via `calculate_stereo_view_offset_(true_index + 1, ...)` at line 6819. The result: both the actual left eye *and* whatever view got miscounted end up carrying the same (left) HMD pose — visually presenting as "the left eye attaches to the HMD" (i.e., it stops responding independently / the other eye is the one that desyncs).

This is intermittent/context-dependent because it only manifests on frames where an extra non-stereo scene view gets constructed between your two real stereo passes — which depends on what's on screen (UI, shadow casters, capture actors), matching why it's inconsistent per-encounter.

**Root cause:** eye identity is inferred from call order, not from an authoritative per-view stereo-pass/eye tag, so any extra `FSceneView` construction between the two real eyes desyncs the index.

---

Both bugs share the same underlying pattern: **eye/pass identity is being inferred heuristically (call order, or a one-time empirical dword diff) instead of being read from a stable, verified field on the view itself.** If you want, I can help implement a fix — e.g. re-deriving `true_index`/eye ownership from the resolved `live_stereo_pass_offset`/`stereo_pass_left/right` enum values (which `sceneview_xref` already computes) instead of call-order counting, and validating `eye_fields` against the *live* stereo-pass field per-frame rather than trusting a single snapshot — but let me know if you want to go there before I touch code.

Build succeeds. Here's a summary of the actual fix:

## Root cause found

`calculate_stereo_view_offset()` uses **shared static heuristic state** (`index_starts_from_one` / `index_was_ever_two`) to guess which eye (`true_index`) a raw `view_index` refers to. This heuristic is meant only to classify the engine's own ambiguous per-eye calls.

However, the Scene View Extension / SplitScreen compatibility path in `sceneview_constructor()` calls `calculate_stereo_view_offset_()` **manually**, already knowing the correct eye — it passes `view_index = true_index + 1` explicitly. That manual call was being fed through the exact same shared heuristic and was also **mutating** that heuristic's static state (`index_was_ever_two`, `index_starts_from_one`). Since both the real engine calls and the manual compatibility-path calls shared one static state machine, whichever call happened first each session could flip the heuristic for the other, silently inverting which eye a manual pose write actually landed on — explaining exactly your symptom: one eye locked to raw HMD orientation (its manual pose write went to the wrong slot / got skipped by the "is_full_pass" early-return), while the other tracked the camera correctly.

## Fix applied

In `src/mods/vr/FFakeStereoRenderingHook.cpp` (`calculate_stereo_view_offset`):
1. Added `is_manual_call` (reads `g_hook->m_inside_manual_view_offset`, already set correctly around the manual call site).
2. Manual calls no longer mutate `index_starts_from_one`/`index_was_ever_two`, and no longer trigger the `is_full_pass` treatment — they're excluded from the heuristic entirely.
3. `true_index` for a manual call is now decoded directly as `view_index - 1` (unambiguous, since the caller computed it), instead of going through the parity heuristic.
4. Added a throttled `[VR][SVC-MANUAL-CALL]` log line that also prints what the old heuristic would have produced, so the next capture can directly confirm whether/how often the two disagreed.

Build succeeded. Please test in-game with Scene View Extension compatibility on and grab a fresh log — the `SVC-MANUAL-CALL` line will show if the heuristic was indeed flipping eye identity, and whether the left eye now tracks correctly.

1. Read FFakeStereoRenderingHook.cpp, lines 6880-6920 :white_check_mark:
## What Scene View Compatibility actually does

Looking at the code path around `sceneview_constructor()` (lines ~6818-6890), here's the pipeline problem it solves:

**Normal UEVR pipeline:** UEVR primarily relies on `ISceneViewExtension`/the game's own stereo-rendering `IStereoRendering` interface calling `calculate_stereo_view_offset()` for each eye, which is the "proper" per-eye pose/projection hook point that most UE games use.

**The problem this game has:** Wuthering Waves apparently constructs its stereo views through a path more like split-screen/`ULocalPlayer::CalcSceneView` — i.e., the engine builds each eye's `FSceneView` directly via `FSceneView`'s constructor with already-baked-in `view_rect`, `view_rotation_matrix`, and `projection_matrix` values from its own (non-VR) split-screen logic, rather than going through the normal per-eye stereo-rendering interface UEVR hooks by default. In that scenario, without Scene View compatibility, the eyes would get whatever pose the engine's split-screen/monoscopic logic computed — not correct VR head/eye offsets.

**What the code does (lines 6818-6890) when the toggle is on:**
1. Guards on `!is_confirmed_non_eye_pass` so it only touches views actually confirmed to be a real left/right eye (via the `sceneview_xref`-resolved stereo pass).
2. Computes the correct viewport rect for that eye (`x += w` for the right eye when NSF isn't already handling that).
3. Calls `calculate_stereo_view_offset_(true_index + 1, ...)` — the manual-call wrapper we were just debugging — to get UEVR's real HMD-eye rotation/position offset for that eye instead of the engine's own value.
4. Converts that back into engine-space rotation matrix and directly overwrites `init_options_view_rotation_matrix`/`init_options_projection_matrix` (or the UE5 equivalents) and the view rect on the `FSceneViewInitOptions` **before** the real constructor runs and bakes them into the `FSceneView`.

In short: **Scene View / SplitScreen compatibility exists to inject UEVR's own per-eye VR pose and projection into engines/games that build their stereo `FSceneView`s through a split-screen-like construction path instead of the standard stereo-rendering interface UEVR normally intercepts.** Without it, on a game like this, the eyes would be positioned by the game's non-VR logic instead of real headset tracking — which is consistent with what you saw (one eye "static"/stuck) before the suppression-toggle bug was fixed and this path was correctly wired up.

Now, let's look at the right-eye shadow fix.
1. Read FFakeStereoRenderingHook.cpp, lines 6470-6580 :white_check_mark:
This is great extra context — it also explains why the earlier `SVC-RAW-STEREO-PASS` values (`2`/`3`) matched `sceneview_xref`'s encoding: `feed()` actively calls `override_offsets(...)` to force `FSceneViewInitOptionsBase::s_stereo_pass_offset` to the **same** offset `sceneview_xref` resolved from the live view, once it can cross-reference them. So once that convergence happens, `get_stereo_pass()` and `sceneview_xref`'s constants are guaranteed consistent — no separate-heuristic risk remains. Good to have that confirmed.

## Now, the right-eye shadow fix (lines 7693-7724)
```cpp
if (vr->is_native_stereo_fix_right_eye_shadows_enabled() && pass2_view != nullptr && nsf_pass2_hacks_safe_this_frame) {
    const auto& fields = sceneview_xref::eye_fields;
    ...
    for (size_t i = 0; i < fields.size(); ++i) {
        if (i < 32 && (mask & (1u << i)) == 0) continue;
        const auto& f = fields[i];
        auto p = (uint32_t*)((uintptr_t)pass2_view + f.offset);
        if (*p == f.right) {
            pass2_restore.emplace_back(p, *p);
            *p = f.left;
        }
    }
}
```

**What problem it addresses:** In NSF (Native Stereo Fix), the game renders the two eyes as two separate passes (`Pass1`=left, `Pass2`=right). World/scene shadow setup is only computed once per frame for the "primary" (shadow-owning) view — normally the left/first eye. When Pass2 (right eye) renders alone, it has no shadow-owning view of its own, so world shadows are missing in the right eye.

**How the fix works:** it takes the live right-eye `FSceneView` (`pass2_view`) and overwrites a set of **empirically-discovered "eye identity" dwords** — fields whose value differs between left (`f.left`) and right (`f.right`) eyes in a snapshot comparison (found once by `sceneview_xref` diffing two constructed views byte-by-byte, see lines 6495-6517) — so that any dword currently holding the "right" value gets flipped to the "left" value. This effectively tricks the engine into treating the right-eye view as if it were the shadow-owning (left) view for shadow-lookup purposes, then restores the original values afterward (`pass2_restore`) so the eye's actual rendering identity isn't otherwise corrupted.

**Why it's flagged as "inconsistent" (per the earlier note in your conversation):**
- `eye_fields` is a **one-time snapshot diff** — it's captured once (probably at startup/first stereo init) by comparing two constructed `FSceneView`s and just recording every dword that differed and looked plausible (not pointer-like, not null-on-right). It has no semantic understanding of *what* each field actually is (StereoPass enum copy? view index? some other per-eye state?), it's purely "this byte differed between L and R that one time."
- Because it's a snapshot, if the actual live value of any of those fields changes across frames/game-modes for reasons unrelated to eye identity (e.g. some other per-frame counter that coincidentally also differed by left/right at snapshot time), flipping it can either fail to have the desired effect (some frames the "right" value isn't even what was recorded, so `*p == f.right` never matches, and shadows stay broken) or, contrarily, corrupt live state that isn't actually eye-identity-related (breaking NSF shadows entirely in other frames/modes).
- There's a manual bitmask (`get_diag_nsf_pass2_eye_field_mask()`) to select which of the discovered fields to actually flip, since not all of them are safe/necessary — this itself is evidence the mapping was found empirically by trial and error, not derived from real engine semantics.

**The fix I'd suggest (previously mentioned, larger change):** instead of trusting the one-time snapshot values (`f.left`/`f.right`) forever, re-derive/validate each field's current "left" value **per-frame** from the actual live left-eye view (`views.data[1]`, i.e. `pass1_view`) at the same offset, and copy that live value into Pass2's slot — rather than a captured constant. That way the fix always applies whatever the left eye's view genuinely holds *this frame*, self-correcting for any per-frame drift, rather than betting on a static snapshot staying valid indefinitely.

Would you like me to implement that per-frame-live-copy change to the shadow fix now, or do you want to keep testing SceneView compatibility a bit more first?

## :speech_balloon: GitHub Copilot
No meaningful overhead. Here's the breakdown:

- **Before:** for each of the (typically small, single-digit count) `eye_fields`, one 4-byte read from `pass2_view` and a compare against a cached constant.
- **After:** one 4-byte read from `pass2_view` (right eye) **and** one 4-byte read from `pass1_view` (left eye), then a compare, and a conditional 4-byte write — same as before.

So the only addition is **one extra 4-byte memory read per field, per frame** (from `pass1_view`, which is already resident in cache since the engine itself just wrote/read it while constructing/using that view this same frame). `eye_fields` is typically a handful of entries (single digits, discovered once at startup), so this is a few extra L1-cache-hit reads — on the order of nanoseconds total, happening once per frame only when NSF + the right-eye-shadow-fix toggle are both enabled. This is not measurable against a VR frame budget (usually ~11ms/frame at 90Hz).

The logging call (`SPDLOG_INFO_EVERY_N_SEC(2, ...)`) is unchanged in frequency (throttled to once per 2 seconds), so no additional logging overhead either.

No profiling is needed here — the change only adds a trivial fixed number of extra pointer dereferences on a low-iteration-count loop that already existed.

**The bug:** `sceneview_xref::resolve_live()` is a **one-shot, session-locked capture**. Look at line 6415:

So `eye_fields` is a permanent snapshot of "which offsets differed between the two eyes during the loading/transition state," not "which offsets differ during real gameplay."

Once real gameplay starts, some of those loading-screen-era offsets legitimately stop differing (game state converges/settles), but since the shadow fix only ever iterates the fixed, stale `eye_fields` list captured at loading time (line 7705-7732), it just silently has fewer fields left to flip — and there's no mechanism to discover the *actual* gameplay-time diverging fields it's now missing. - Why it permanently degrades once the map finishes loading and real gameplay fields diverge differently than the loading-screen snapshot did (drops to 3/12 and never recovers).
- Why only a full restart fixes it — `resolve_live()`'s guard clause prevents ever re-resolving in the same process lifetime, and `eye_fields` is never re-populated.

**Proposed fix:** don't permanently lock `eye_fields` from a single early frame. **Why a zero-sync fix isn't physically possible in either pathway:**

The actual root cause isn't a UEVR-side pose cache/read problem at all — it's that **the game engine's own camera (`view_rotation`/`view_location`, driven by the character controller/animation blueprint) genuinely advances/ticks in the real time gap between the left-eye render call and the right-eye render call**, whether that gap is NSF's Pass1→Pass2 or SVC's two manual calls. We don't control engine tick timing between those two calls. So there is no way to make the two eyes naturally "already agree" without forcing them to — caching+syncing one eye's pose onto the other is the *only* mechanism that can work, in any pathway, given this root cause. What we *can* do is stop reimplementing that mechanism per-pathway and give it one shared implementation, so SVC gets the same protection NSF already has, instead of being an unpatched gap.

**Proposed unified design:**

## What changed
Added a new experimental diagnostic toggle: **"DIAG: Treat View Index 1 As Monoscopic (experimental)"** (in the same VR settings panel as the other NSF diagnostics, right after "DIAG: Suppressed View Index").

- It's **off by default**, so nothing changes until you enable it.

## How to test the hypothesis
1. Launch the game, enable **"DIAG: Treat View Index 1 As Monoscopic (experimental)"**.
2. Reproduce the double vision scenario (both with NSF on and with Scene View Compatibility/NSF off, since you said the symptom appears in both).
